## The challenge is written twice, deliberately

`assert/0.1` says `proof.challenge` must be the paired `challengeId`, and
that this is what "stops one captured and replayed into another". In W3C Data
Integrity that holds because the proof options are canonicalised with the
document, so `challenge` is signed.

`affinidi_data_integrity` has no `challenge` proof option, and the VTC
verifies over the presentation with the whole `proof` block removed. A value
written only there is therefore **not covered by the signature** — swapping
it on a captured presentation would go unnoticed.

So `build_presentation` writes the challenge to `proof.challenge` (what the
spec names) and to top-level `nonce` (what the signature covers), and the VTC
requires both to agree. `the_signed_nonce_is_covered_by_the_proof` pins that
tampering with `nonce` breaks verification — which is the whole reason it
carries the challenge, and the reason neither copy can be dropped as
redundant.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.g@affinidi.com>

* feat: read the community's personhood replies, and refuse a match-code disagreement

The two verbs could be sent but not understood: replies arrived as
`#response` documents that nothing parsed, so a member never learned the
challenge id to sign against.

`parse_challenge_reply` and `parse_assert_reply` normalise both reply
shapes the VTC produces — the dispatcher's `#response` document with members
under `payload`, and a hand-built bare body — the same way `messaging`
already does, which also makes them transport-agnostic: a TSP frame carries
the response document raw.

Routing needed no change; `OPENVTC_CATCH_ALL_PATTERN` already admits
`https://trusttasks.org/spec/vtc/.*`.

The challenge parser compares the community's own copy of the match code
against the one derived locally and treats a disagreement as an error. The
two are computed by different implementations, and a drift is otherwise
invisible: both sides still show eight plausible characters, so the people in
the room conclude they have the wrong ceremony rather than that the software
disagrees with itself. A community that sends no copy at all is fine — the
code is derived locally, so an older VTC costs nothing.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.g@affinidi.com>

* feat: drive the personhood ceremony from the communities panel

The library surface had no way in. `p` on an Active membership asks the
community for a challenge; the reply lands as the panel's live challenge and
shows the match code; `P` answers it.

The match code gets its own line in the panel's emphasis colour rather than
being folded into the status text — it is the thing a member reads aloud, and
a code that has to be picked out of a sentence is a code that gets misread.

An expired challenge renders as expired rather than disappearing. A member
who has just been read a code, looking at a panel that never mentions one,
cannot tell "it lapsed" from "it never arrived".

Key hints are gated exactly as the handler gates the keys, which is this
file's existing discipline: `p` on Active rows only, `P` only while a live
challenge is in hand. Both would otherwise be dead keys — the defect that
gating was written to remove.

The assertion targets the membership the *challenge* names, not the
highlighted row. Answering against whichever row happens to be selected is
exactly the confusion the stored `vtc_did` exists to prevent. It presents
that membership's own credentials and lets the community's policy choose:
a client-side filter would have to guess at a policy it cannot read, and
guessing wrong withholds the very credential that would have satisfied it.
Scoping to the one membership also keeps one community's credentials from
being disclosed to another.

Two supporting changes:

- `Verb` gained the two personhood sends, so `CommunityOutcome`'s
  `leaving: bool` became a `Performed` enum. A boolean cannot say which of
  four things happened, and the arms that got it wrong would have told the
  member the wrong thing went wrong rather than failed.
- The three out-params of `process_inbound_message` became `InboundEffects`.
  The live challenge belongs to `State`, not the account, so it is reported
  up rather than persisted — a single-use nonce with a ten-minute life has no
  business surviving a restart.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.g@affinidi.com>

title: feat(vtc)!: reach personhood over messaging, and bind its challenge to something signed
body:
Follow-up to #1085. Companion client PR: **OpenVTC/openvtc#257**.

Personhood was REST-only. `openvtc` — which talks to communities over DIDComm and TSP and holds no bearer token — could not run the ceremony at all, so the member half of the feature had no client that could reach it.

## Reachable over messaging

`members/personhood/{challenge,assert}` now route through the messaging Trust Task dispatcher alongside the join verbs, which also makes them reachable over TSP (the TSP inbound path hands every frame to the same dispatcher).

The route handlers keep their bodies in `challenge_inner` / `assert_inner`, which both transports call. Two implementations of one ceremony is a security difference nothing tests.

Each verb carries its own caller gate, because "an authenticated session" — what the REST routes rest on — has no equivalent on a transport that only proves who sent the bytes:

| Verb | Gate | Why |
|---|---|---|
| `challenge` | caller must be a member | Otherwise anyone who can reach the mediator could mint challenges against this community's members. The *subject* may be another member — that is the in-person ceremony. |
| `assert` | sender must **be** the subject | `assert/0.1` declares `exposure.actsAsSubject: true` — "the asserting member is the subject … exercising their own authority over their own personhood state". |

Minting a challenge for someone else confers nothing: the nonce is bound to the subject, and only a presentation signed by that subject's key can spend it.

## The challenge was not bound to anything

`assert/0.1` §Authorization says the challenge binding "establishes that this presentation was made for this exchange, and is what stops one captured and replayed into another". In W3C Data Integrity that holds because the proof options are canonicalised with the document, so `challenge` is signed.

`affinidi_data_integrity`'s `DataIntegrityProof` **has no `challenge` field**, and `verify_vp_proof` verifies over the presentation with the whole `proof` block removed. So `proof.challenge` was **unsigned**.

Anyone holding a captured presentation — a relaying mediator, anyone with log access — could mint a fresh challenge for that member, swap the one unsigned field, and replay it. The signature still verified, because it had never covered the challenge. For a flag whose revocation is an administrative act, that means a revoked assertion could be restored without the member's participation.

The challenge must now also appear at top-level `nonce`, which is outside the proof block and therefore covered by the holder's signature, and the two copies must agree. This is what the published task already says the binding does; it just did not do it.

Two tests pin it from both sides: a presentation with no signed `nonce` is refused, and one whose unsigned `proof.challenge` has been swapped away from its signed `nonce` is refused.

> [!WARNING]
> **BREAKING CHANGE**: a personhood presentation without a top-level `nonce` equal to `proof.challenge` is refused. No client produced one — `openvtc` had no personhood support and `vtc-client` only reads the flag — so nothing in the ecosystem is affected, and OpenVTC/openvtc#257 emits both copies.

## Match-code vector

Pins `5CY1-GZEE`, which `openvtc-core` pins too. The two derivations agree only because they compute the same digest over the same bytes, and nothing else would catch them drifting: a changed domain tag or alphabet on either side still yields eight plausible characters that simply never match, which reads to the two people in the room as "wrong ceremony" rather than "your software disagrees with itself".

## Verification

Rebased onto merged `main` (so it includes #1082's response-shape changes) and re-run there:

- `cargo test -p vtc-service` — 40 test binaries, 0 failures
- `cargo clippy -p vtc-service --all-targets` — clean
- `cargo fmt --check` — clean

Three new dispatcher tests cover the messaging path: a member mints a challenge and gets the match code back, a non-member is refused, and one member cannot assert for another.

title: feat(vtc): let a community vet a member in person and have it count as personhood evidence
body:
Personhood already shipped, and it already matches DTG Credentials: a PHC is a VMC, and `new_vmc(personhood: true)` appends `PersonhoodCredential` exactly as the spec's worked example shows. What was missing was the ceremony an operator actually performs — meeting someone, satisfying themselves the DID in front of them is theirs, and having that count.

The default `personhood.rego` accepted one evidence shape: a `WitnessCredential` from some third party. An administrator who did the verifying themselves had nowhere to put it.

## The community's own vetting becomes evidence

DTG Credentials §Identity Verification Credentials defines an IDVC as "any W3C VC satisfying a VTC/VTN's identity-proofing requirements" and explicitly *not* a `DTGCredential` subtype, so a community acting as its own identity-verification provider needs no new credential type. Registering `IdentityVerification` as an endorsement type and issuing it per member reuses `vtc/endorsement-types/register/0.1` and `vtc/endorsements/issue/0.1` verbatim — **no new Trust Task family**, and revocation comes free via the community's existing status list.

`vtc/members/personhood/assert/0.1` is untouched, which was the constraint worth respecting: its Authorization section is explicit that holder-equality and challenge-binding are both load-bearing and neither substitutes for the other. An admin-asserts-directly path would have had to bypass the presentation the task requires, so the vetting is evidence the member presents rather than a gate the admin steps around.

## Three bindings, each with a test that breaks exactly one

| Binding | Why |
|---|---|
| `issuer == community_did` | An endorsement type is a *name*, not an authority. Without this, any issuer anywhere could mint a credential typed `IdentityVerification` and unlock personhood here. This is why `community_did` is now in the policy input at all. |
| `credentialSubject.id == applicant_did` | The route's holder-match binds the presenter; this binds the credential, so a member cannot present a vetting record issued about somebody else. |
| the endorsement type | A role VEC is community-issued and names the member too, so without the type check every member holding a role credential satisfies the policy — which is every member. |

Two further tests run a credential from the **real builder** through the **real extractor** into the **real policy**. Every other test in that file hand-writes `vp_claims`, so they all agree about a shape none of them obtained from the code that produces it; if `build_custom_endorsement` moved `endorsement` out of `credentialSubject`, they would all keep passing while every vetting in production was denied.

## The spoken match code

`challengeId` is a UUID — fine on a wire, hopeless read aloud — so the challenge response now carries eight Crockford base32 characters derived from it (no `I`/`L`/`O`/`U`, nothing mishearable).

It is **derived**, never transmitted as an independent secret and never accepted as one: both parties compute it from the id they already hold and say it to each other. Nothing checks it server-side, because there is nothing it could prove that `proof.challenge` does not already prove. It is a Bluetooth pairing code, not a password.

It rides in `ext` because the response schema is `additionalProperties: false`. A conformance witness now pins that, and the assertion was checked for vacuity — moving the field to the top level does fail the test.

## What this deliberately does not do

**Enforce uniqueness.** DTG Credentials requires governance enforcing both real human personhood *and* exactly one membership per person; this is evidence for the first only. Nothing stops one human joining twice under two DIDs and being vetted twice.

The spec also locates PHC status in **governance and trust registries rather than credential structure** — the `PersonhoodCredential` type is described there as a *non-authoritative hint*, so a verifier following the spec reads the community's governance, not the type array. The VTC publishes no governance statement today.

Both limits are stated in the policy module and in the operator guide rather than left for someone to discover.

## Verification

- `cargo test -p vtc-service` — 30 test binaries, 0 failures
- `cargo check --workspace --all-targets` — clean
- `cargo clippy -p vtc-service --all-targets` — clean
- `cargo fmt --check` — clean

title: spec(vtc): let a member prove they issued the edge they are publishing
body:
Stacks on #258 — please merge that first; the version bumps are sequential.

An edge may be published under a **relationship DID**: an identifier scoped to
one counterparty, which names no member. The community still has to know that a
member published it, and the document's own `proof` says only that a member
*sent* it, not that they control the credential's issuing key.

Without something to close that gap, **any member who was ever handed a VRC
could publish another party's edge.** Issuing a credential and publishing it to
a community's trust graph are different disclosures, and the second is the
issuer's to make.

`pop` is a data-integrity proof by a verification method the VRC's `issuer`
controls, bound to the enclosing document's `id` and to the credential's digest.
Omitted when the VRC's `issuer` *is* the document's issuer, where the document's
own proof already establishes control. Added to both `0.1` and `0.2` so the two
stay aligned; the implementation still binds `0.1`.

## The binding is the document, not a session — and this diverges from the implementation on purpose

The implementation this comes from
(OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure#1061, mine) binds its authorization to
a **REST session id**, plus an audience and a timestamp.

None of the three belongs in a transport-neutral specification, and two are
already framework members: a document carries its own `recipient` and
`issuedAt`, and a session exists only on one binding.

What the authorization actually needs is to be unreplayable into a *different
document*, and every document carries a unique `id` (SPEC §4.3). Binding to that
is **stricter** than binding to a session — a session covers many documents —
and it is available on every transport.

So this PR publishes what the implementation *should* do rather than what it
does. That leaves the implementation diverging from this schema until it
follows, and I would rather have that written down than standardise a REST
detail into a transport-neutral spec. If the WG disagrees and would rather the
schema describe what ships today, say so and I will change it — but I think
that would be the wrong way round.

## One consumer requirement the schema cannot carry

**A consumer MUST NOT retain the authorization after verifying it.**

It answers one question at one moment. Storing it accumulates a durable link
between the publishing member and a relationship DID that names nobody —
precisely the correlation that publishing under a relationship DID exists to
avoid. No schema can express "do not keep this", so the prose does.

## Not breaking

An optional member on a payload that previously forbade it. Every document that
validated before still validates.

## Verified

- `npm run validate` — 344 specs, 64 shared schemas
- `npm run check-bindings` — 344 specs against 344 TS and 339 Rust modules, all agree
- `cargo fmt --all --check`, `cargo build`, `cargo test -p trust-tasks-rs` — clean

`trust-tasks-rs` 0.11.6 → 0.11.7, `trust-tasks-ts` 0.12.6 → 0.12.7, with the
changelog entry.

title: feat(sdk): extract the agent-side connect ladder into vta_sdk::agent_connect
body:
Every tool that runs *beside* a user and talks to their VTA on their behalf needs the same four ways in — did:webvh bundle, scoped did:key, bearer token, existing `pnm` session — in the same order, with the same fail-fast rules. That ladder existed only inside `vta-mcp`'s `main.rs`, so the next bridge had to copy 110 lines or invent a fifth way in.

`vta_sdk::agent_connect::AgentConnect` is that ladder as SDK surface.

- `mode()` resolves the rung with **no I/O**, so a bridge can log it — and refuse a rung it does not support — before connecting. `ConnectMode::is_dedicated_agent()` makes the operator-vs-agent distinction available to callers deciding whether to enroll as a managed device.
- `connect()` returns the authenticated `VtaClient`.
- Session mode keeps `TransportChoice::Auto`, so it inherits the workspace preference order (TSP > DIDComm > REST) from what both DID documents advertise.

Two rules are **enforced rather than documented**, both carried over from the `vta-mcp` original:

1. The two DIDComm identity modes are mutually exclusive — a bundle *and* a did:key is an error, not a silent precedence win.
2. A half-configured rung errors naming the missing fields instead of falling through to session mode. A bridge silently authenticating as the operator rather than as its scoped agent identity is the failure this exists to prevent, and there is a test asserting the error mentions the gap and *not* the session.

`vta-mcp` is refactored onto it, which is what proves the extraction: `build_client` is now a pure args → `AgentConnect` mapping plus a connect, and its tests assert which rung a set of flags selects — something the old inline ladder had no way to test.

## Motivation

The first consumer beyond `vta-mcp` is an agent-memory service (a Claude Code plugin over `vta/memory/*`), which needs exactly these four rungs and nothing else. It currently pulls `vta-sdk` from this branch via `[patch.crates-io]`.

## Testing

- 10 new unit tests on `agent_connect` covering rung selection, precedence, mutual exclusion, half-configuration, empty-token fall-through, and bundle loading from a path or inline JSON.
- 4 new tests in `vta-mcp` mapping CLI flags to rungs.
- `cargo clippy` clean on both crates.

title: spec(vtc): publish the refusal an applicant is entitled to, and let them ask without an id
body:
A community can refuse a join request for a stated reason and then have no way
to tell the applicant what it was. Three tasks send the refusal detail today
and none of their schemas define it.

Second batch from the conformance witness in
OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure#1076.

## `JoinRequest.decision`

`code`, optional `reason`, `decidedAt`.

Deliberately **distinct from `policyDecision`**: that one records the
community's internal verdict, while this is written by *both* rejection paths —
a policy auto-deny at submit and an admin's later refusal — so a client reads
one shape instead of reconciling two.

`code` is stable and safe to branch on. `decidedAt` is when the decision was
taken, **not** when the poll answering it was produced; on an admin refusal the
two diverge by however long the applicant takes to ask.

## `JoinRequest.vpClaims`

The canonical projection of the applicant's presentation, extracted at submit
and used as the input the community's join policy reads. Opaque here — its
members are whatever that policy asks for.

Because the component carries `additionalProperties: false`, those two absent
properties put **three** tasks off their own schemas at once:
`join-requests/list`, `join-requests/show`, `join-requests/status`.

## `status/0.1`: the refusal members, and an optional `requestId`

The poll is the request an applicant actually makes, so it gains the three
refusal members directly.

`requestId` becomes **optional**. An applicant whose first reply was lost never
received an id; a poll resolved from their own authenticated DID is the only
form available to them, and *a refusal they cannot ask about is a refusal they
cannot act on*. A consumer given the id MUST prefer it over inferring the
request from the caller.

## One consumer requirement, stated rather than implied

The refusal members MUST NOT be returned for any status other than `rejected`.
They assert that a decision was taken, and emitting them beside a `pending`
status would tell an applicant they had been refused when they had not. That is
in the prose, not just the schema.

## Not breaking

Two optional members added to schemas that previously forbade them, and one
required member relaxed — every document that validated before still validates.
A consumer that assumed `requestId` was always present now has a case to
handle, which is the point of the change.

## How this one hid

Worth recording: only a **rejected** request carries these members. A witness
built from a pending poll conforms, and would have passed green over the whole
divergence. The drift is conditional, which is why it survived a suite that
otherwise checks this task.

## Verified

- `npm run validate` — 344 specs, 64 shared schemas
- `npm run check-bindings` — 344 specs against 344 TS and 339 Rust modules, all agree
- `cargo fmt --all --check`, `cargo build`, `cargo test -p trust-tasks-rs` — clean
- 9 files changed, no codegen churn: regeneration is diff-stable when
  `cargo fmt` follows it, as #257 established

`trust-tasks-rs` 0.11.5 → 0.11.6, `trust-tasks-ts` 0.12.5 → 0.12.6, with the
changelog entry.

As with #257, I cannot verify this end to end from the implementation side:
`verifiable-trust-infrastructure` pins `trust-tasks-rs` from crates.io, so
those drift entries stay recorded there until a release carries this.

title: fix(mcp): look the pnm session up under the key pnm actually writes
body:
`vta-mcp --vta <slug>` — the invocation its own README documents — could never find a session.

`pnm` stores every login under the keyring key **`vta:<slug>`** (`vta_keyring_key` in `pnm-cli/src/config.rs`); `cnm` uses `community:<slug>` for the same reason. Neither session backend adds a prefix on the way in or out — `keyring.rs` passes the key straight to `Entry::new`, `file.rs` uses it verbatim as a map key. `vta-mcp` passed the **bare slug**, so the lookup missed.

**The operator sees an authentication failure.** That is the part worth fixing rather than documenting around: it is indistinguishable, from their side, from an expired login. They run `pnm auth status`, are told they are fine, and are none the wiser.

## The fix

One definition of the rule — `vta_sdk::agent_connect::pnm_session_key` — placed next to the connect ladder both agent-side bridges already share. It is idempotent, so an operator who worked the bug out for themselves and passes `vta:mine` keeps working.

## How it surfaced

Building a second consumer of `agent_connect` (an agent-memory service) hit exactly this, which is also why the helper belongs in the SDK rather than in either bridge: there are now two callers and the rule is `pnm`'s, not theirs.

## Testing

`cargo test -p vta-sdk --lib agent_connect` — 11 pass, one new covering the prefix, idempotency, and that a `community:` key is not mistaken for an already-prefixed VTA key. `cargo test -p vta-mcp` — 5 pass; the session-mode test now pins `vta:my-vta`. Clippy clean on both. README corrected.

title: fix(vtc)!: return the response shapes the specs publish
body:
Third batch of the 33, applying the standing direction — **build to spec, not
to what has been built.** Drift **31 → 27**.

Five handlers, all the same kind of defect: each had every value its schema
asks for and replied with something narrower.

| Task | Was | Now |
|---|---|---|
| `backup/export` | bare `BackupEnvelope` | `{envelope: …}` |
| `members/removed` | top-level array | `{removed: […]}` |
| `website/files/delete` | 200, zero bytes | `{path, deleted}` |
| `website/rollback` | 200, zero bytes | `{generation, current, noop}` |
| `endorsements/revoke` | `{id}` | `{endorsementId, revocation: {credentialId, revokedAt}, statusListIndex}` |

`endorsements/revoke` is the one worth looking at: all four members were in
hand. The handler bound `updated` and threw it away with `let _ = updated;`
one line before replying. The idempotent no-op path now answers with the same
shape, reading the timestamp already on the row rather than inventing one.

## Two things the witness taught me that reading would not have

**`website/rollback` types `current` as a boolean and `generation` as a
string.** `current` answers *"did the rollback take"*, not *"which generation is
live"* — I wrote it as the generation number, twice, and the sweep rejected
both. The string typing matches the path segment the spec declares. I would
have shipped an integer called `current` and been confident about it.

**`website/generations/list` is not envelope-only, and its own entry said it
was.** The missing wrapper is fixed here, but the rows diverge too: the spec's
row carries `generation` and `current`, while the service sends `isCurrent` and
adds `deployedAt` and `sizeBytes`. It stays a drift entry with the diagnosis
corrected — one rename belongs here, and two members worth having belong
upstream rather than being dropped.

So one of the 33 notes was wrong about its own shape. Worth knowing when
reading the rest of the table.

## A limit worth restating

The witness compares a **hand-transcribed fixture** with its schema. It proves
the fixture conforms; it does not prove the handler emits the fixture. That is
the transcription gap #1076 documented as its own mutation #6.

The integration tests are the other half, and they did their job — `members_crud`
read the removed list as a bare array in two places and failed until updated.

## Verified

- `cargo test -p vtc-service` — 53 suites, 0 failures
- `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets -- -D warnings` — clean
- `cargo fmt --all --check` — clean

## Breaking

`POST /v1/backup/export`, `GET /v1/members/removed`,
`DELETE /v1/website/files/{path}`, `POST /v1/website/rollback/{gen}` and
`DELETE /v1/credentials/endorsements/{id}` return the shapes their published
schemas declare. Every one was previously returning something the schema did
not describe.

## What is left

**27.** The remaining `HERE` entry is `auth/admin_session`, which returns 204
and puts its result in two `Set-Cookie` headers where the spec requires
`{sessionId, expiresAt}` — a real behaviour change for the admin SPA, so it
wants its own PR rather than riding along here.

questions on the install-claim flow, and 6 I have not classified yet.

title: fix(vtc)!: return the response shapes the specs publish (#1082)
body:
fix(vtc)!: return the response shapes the specs publish (#1082)

Four of the divergences #1076 recorded, all of the same kind: the handler had
every value the schema asks for and replied with something narrower.

- `backup/export` returned the bare `BackupEnvelope`; the spec wraps it as
  `{envelope: …}`. The inner object always conformed member for member.
- `members/removed` returned a top-level array; the spec says
  `{removed: […]}`. The rows always conformed.
- `website/files/delete` returned 200 with zero bytes, discarding the `path`
  and the outcome the spec asks for as `{path, deleted}`.
- `website/rollback` returned 200 with zero bytes, having already computed the
  `noop` the spec asks for — it is the same `from != gen_num` test that decides
  whether to write an audit event.
- `endorsements/revoke` replied `{id}` where the spec requires
  `{endorsementId, revocation: {credentialId, revokedAt}, statusListIndex}`.
  All four were in hand: the handler bound `updated` and threw it away with
  `let _ = updated;`. The idempotent no-op path answers with the same shape,
  reading the timestamp already on the row rather than inventing one.

Two things the witness taught me that reading would not have.

**`website/rollback` types `current` as a boolean and `generation` as a
string.** `current` answers "did the rollback take", not "which generation is
live" — I had written it as the generation number, twice, and the sweep
rejected both. The string typing matches the path segment the spec declares.

**`website/generations/list` is not envelope-only, and its entry said it was.**
The missing `{generations: […]}` wrapper is fixed here, but the rows diverge
too: the spec's row carries `generation` and `current` where the service sends
`isCurrent` and adds `deployedAt` and `sizeBytes`. It stays a drift entry, with
the diagnosis corrected — one rename belongs here, and two members worth having
belong upstream rather than being dropped.

Drift count 31 → 27.

A limit worth restating: the witness compares a hand-transcribed fixture with
its schema, so it proves the fixture conforms, not that the handler emits the
fixture. The integration tests are the other half, and two of them had to move
here — `members_crud` read the removed list as a bare array in two places.

BREAKING CHANGE: `POST /v1/backup/export`, `GET /v1/members/removed`,
`DELETE /v1/website/files/{path}`, `POST /v1/website/rollback/{gen}` and
`DELETE /v1/credentials/endorsements/{id}` return the shapes their published
schemas declare. Every one of them was previously returning something the
schema did not describe.

Refs #1059

title: spec(vtc): publish the community's relationship-identifier default, and what an update changed
body:
Three VTC tasks send members these schemas do not define, and two of them are
one missing property.

Found by the conformance witness in
OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure#1076 — the first thing on either side
of the boundary to compare a response with the schema its URI publishes. It
recorded 33 divergences; these are three of them, and the only three whose root
cause is a single absent property.

## `relationshipIdentifierDefault`

Declares which identifier form a community expects members to issue
relationship credentials under:

- **`attributed`** — the member's membership DID, so an edge names them. What a
  public community (an open-source project, say) reasonably wants.
- **`pairwise`** — a relationship DID unique to each counterparty. What DTG
  Credentials recommends.

It is a **declaration, not an enforcement**. The member still chooses per
relationship, and a community that wants to *require* one form does so in its
own policy. The value exists so a client can read what the community expects
**before** minting, rather than discovering it from a rejection.

It was added to the implementation in
OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure#1061 and never brought here. That is the
whole defect — this PR is me closing my own gap.

Because `CommunityProfile` and `CommunityProfileSnapshot` both carry
`additionalProperties: false`, one absent property drifted three tasks:
`community/profile/update`, `config/export`, and `config/import` — the last
because an import replays the document an export produced.

## `fieldsChanged`

On the update response: names the members the patch actually changed, in their
wire spelling, empty when the submitted values matched what was stored. It lets
a caller tell a no-op from an applied change without diffing the returned
profile against the one it sent.

## Not breaking, and edited in place

Both are `status: draft` edits made in place, per CONTRIBUTING-SPECS §Version
rules. Each **adds** an optional member to a schema that previously forbade it,
so any document that validated before still validates.

## One consumer requirement worth stating rather than implying

Reject a `relationshipIdentifierDefault` outside the two defined values instead
of storing it. The value is published to clients, and one they cannot interpret
is worse than no declaration at all. That is in the prose, not just the `enum`.

## On the generated-bindings diff

Regenerated for the four affected specs only — `community/profile/show`,
`community/profile/update`, `config/export`, `config/import`.

A full `cargo run -p trust-tasks-codegen` also **reformats all 339 Rust
modules**: my local formatter wraps differently from whichever produced the
committed ones. The 335 files whose only change was that reformatting are
reverted, so this diff is not 343 files of churn.

The four kept files still carry some of that reformatting mixed with the real
change. They are generated artifacts, and hand-editing them to shrink the diff
would make them disagree with what the codegen emits — which is a worse problem
than a noisy diff. Flagging it so a reviewer knows why ~870 lines moved for two
new properties.

If the project would rather pin the formatter so regeneration is diff-stable,
that seems worth doing on its own — it will hit every contributor who
regenerates, not just this PR.

## Verified

- `npm run validate` — 344 specs validated, 64 shared schemas indexed
- `npm run check-bindings` — 344 specs against 344 TS and 339 Rust modules, all agree
- `npm run build-ts-bindings`, `cargo run -p trust-tasks-codegen`
- `cargo build -p trust-tasks-rs`, `cargo test -p trust-tasks-rs` — clean

One thing I could **not** verify end to end: `verifiable-trust-infrastructure`
pins `trust-tasks-rs` from crates.io, so the three drift entries stay recorded
there until a release carries this. I have not claimed them closed on that side.

title: feat(sdk): extract the agent-side connect ladder into vta_sdk::agent_connect (#1081)
body:
feat(sdk): extract the agent-side connect ladder into vta_sdk::agent_connect (#1081)

* feat(sdk): extract the agent-side connect ladder into vta_sdk::agent_connect

Every tool that runs beside a user and talks to their VTA on their behalf
needs the same four ways in — did:webvh bundle, scoped did:key, bearer
token, existing pnm session — in the same order, with the same fail-fast
rules. That ladder existed only inside vta-mcp's main.rs, so the next
bridge had to copy 110 lines or invent a fifth way in.

`AgentConnect` is that ladder as SDK surface. `mode()` resolves the rung
with no I/O, so a bridge can log it (and refuse a rung it does not
support) before connecting; `connect()` returns the authenticated
VtaClient. Session mode keeps TransportChoice::Auto, so it inherits the
workspace preference order (TSP > DIDComm > REST) from what both DID
documents advertise.

Two rules are enforced rather than documented, both carried over from the
vta-mcp original: the two DIDComm identity modes are mutually exclusive,
and a half-configured rung errors naming the missing fields instead of
falling through to session mode — a bridge silently authenticating as the
operator rather than as its scoped agent identity is the failure that
matters here. ConnectMode::is_dedicated_agent() makes the same
distinction available to callers deciding whether to enroll as a device.

vta-mcp is refactored onto it, which is what proves the extraction: its
build_client is now a pure args -> AgentConnect mapping plus a connect,
and its tests assert which rung a set of flags selects.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.g@affinidi.com>

* docs(vta): document agent memory in the personal-AI-agents guide

The guide walks an operator from transports through identity, ACL, wake,
step-up and credentials, and never mentions the store that is the reason
most agents want a VTA in the first place. `vta/memory/{put,list,delete}/0.1`
has shipped, is context-gated and audited, and appears in no operator doc.

Adds a step covering it, and states the two boundaries up front because
both are easy to get wrong and expensive to unwind: memory is not the
secrets/credential vault (those are capability-gated), and memory is not
application state (no version, no cursor — and 'forget everything' has to
stay safe to ask). Also records the retrieval consequence of the task's
whole-context list, since that is the client's problem and the design note
for it lives elsewhere.

Also notes agent_connect in the vta-mcp README, so the four auth modes it
documents are attributed to the SDK rather than read as its own.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.gore@gmail.com>

title: fix(vtc)!: accept the install flow's own field names
body:
Second batch of the 33. Closes one more entry, but the reason it matters is a
live bug rather than a conformance count.

## The install flow disagreed with itself

`claim/finish` derives `ClaimFinishResponse` **with** `rename_all`, so it
returns `setupSessionToken`. `admin/bootstrap` derived `BootstrapRequest`
**without** one, so it demanded `setup_session_token`.

The service handed a caller one spelling and required the other back.

Only the admin SPA survived it, because `Install.tsx:217` re-keyed the value by
hand between the two calls:

```ts
{ setup_session_token: finishBody.setupSessionToken }
```

**A client written from the published schema could not complete an install at
all** — its body deserialised as a missing required field. The schema has said
`setupSessionToken` all along.

`ClaimStartRequest` and `ClaimFinishRequest` had the same gap, so
`install_token`, `claim_secret`, `registration_id` and `webauthn_response` were
snake_case against schemas naming them in camelCase.

## What changed

All three request structs gain `rename_all = "camelCase"`, and the SPA now
passes the token straight through instead of translating it.

Drift count **32 → 31**. `admin/bootstrap` is promoted to `checked!`. The two
install/claim entries stay, rewritten to describe only what is left of them:
`claimSecret` is a real member the spec does not define, and the response omits
`didBindingChallenge`, which the spec requires because this service binds the
admin DID at `claim/finish` instead. Those are a spec-and-flow reconciliation,
not a casing fix, and they are not attempted here.

## One thing I got wrong and reverted

A first pass swept `RegisterFinishRequest` (`routes/admin/passkeys.rs`) up with
the rest — it is also snake_case. The tests caught it: `register/finish` started
returning 422.

Reverted. It is a different endpoint with its own drift entry, and widening
this change to cover it would have buried a decision inside a mechanical fix.
`install_flow.rs` exercises both flows and now shows the two casings side by
side, with a comment saying why.

## The pattern, third time today

R3.1 casing, after the `Verifiable`-prefixed credential tags (#1071) and the
`Paginated<T>` wrapper (#1078). The common thread is not carelessness about
casing — it is that **a request struct's serde attributes were never compared
to the schema its URI publishes**. The witness from #1076 is the first thing in
this repo that does that, and it has now found three.

## Verified

- `cargo test -p vtc-service` — 53 suites, 0 failures
- `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets -- -D warnings` — clean
- `cargo fmt --all --check` — clean
- `tsc -b --noEmit` in `admin-ui` — clean

## Breaking

`POST /v1/install/claim/start`, `/v1/install/claim/finish` and
`/v1/admin/bootstrap` accept camelCase request members and reject the
snake_case names they previously required. Any caller that worked before did so
by disagreeing with the published schema.

title: Cross-artifact lifecycle precedence: suspension, supersession, restoration
body:
## Summary

#1075 fixed an instance: an expired VRC became a permanent edge because the
relationship route read neither `validFrom` nor `validUntil`. It did not fix the
class. Nothing in this workspace establishes **precedence between a
cryptographically valid but stale artifact and a later lifecycle event**, and
several credential types have no lifecycle vocabulary at all beyond "exists" and
"deleted".

Filing the general problem so the instance fix does not stand in for it.

## Why the instance was reachable

Two defensible decisions composed into an unreachable state:

1. The relationship graph is read **without re-checking dates**. Reasonable on
   its own — the edge was validated at ingress.
2. A VRC carries **no `credentialStatus`**, per planning-review D7. Also
   reasonable, and deliberately so: a status-list host learns which verifier
   checked which credential and when, which is the correlation the pairwise work
   exists to remove.

Neither is wrong. Together they leave `DELETE /v1/relationships/{id}` as the only
removal path, so a valid-forever artifact has no lifecycle at all.

**The deliberate absence of revocation is what makes precedence load-bearing.**
Where a credential type omits status for privacy reasons — which we think is
usually the right call — precedence and effective-time rules become the only
remaining lifecycle mechanism, not a refinement on top of revocation.

## What is missing

No shared vocabulary or precedence rule for:

- **suspension** — temporarily ineffective, not withdrawn
- **supersession** — a later artifact displacing an earlier one
- **restoration** — and its boundary against replacement or fresh grant
- **effective time and event precedence** across composed artifacts
- **transaction-time state discovery**, including what a verifier does when
  discovery is deliberately unavailable because the presentation must carry what
  it needs
- **approval freshness after an authority change** — we re-evaluate approver-set
  membership at execution (`policy_gate.rs`), but nothing re-evaluates an
  approval against a *credential* whose authority has since changed

## Where it already bites

- **VRC** — no status, no suspension; #1075 gated ingress only, and the VIC and
  recognition paths deliberately keep their own window semantics rather than
  sharing the gate. Three paths, three answers.
- **Relationship graph** — since #1073 an edge is complete or half-complete, but
  neither state has a notion of *suspended*. A half-edge whose reciprocal has
  expired is indistinguishable from one that never arrived.
- **VPC** (#1074) — a persona annotation has no lifecycle of its own. Detaching
  is the only reversal, and there is no record that a correlation once existed
  and was withdrawn.
- **VDC**, when it lands — this is where it gets expensive. A delegation that can
  be suspended and restored is the whole point of a bounded appointment, and the
  design note already commits us to freshness-by-re-issuance rather than live
  lookup, which puts the entire weight on precedence rules we have not written.

## Proposed shape

1. A common lifecycle vocabulary across credential types, rather than per-type
   ad-hoc handling.
2. Effective-time and precedence rules for composed artifacts — which state
   controls at decision time when two valid artifacts disagree.
3. One transaction-time evaluation gate that every ingress path calls, extending
   `credentials::ingress` where #1075 put the window check, with any deviation
   documented at the call site rather than implied.
4. Explicit restoration-versus-replacement semantics.
5. A statement of what a verifier may conclude when authoritative current state
   is deliberately undiscoverable.

## Provenance

The instance is ours (#1075, conformance-review finding F9). The generalisation
is external: it matches RAHP finding **F-003** in
`sankarshanmukhopadhyay/rahp-toolkit#66`, which arrived at the same residual from
a guardianship/fiduciary pressure test rather than from our code. Evidence from
our instance is posted there.

Note the numbering collision: RAHP's **F-003** and our conformance review's
**F3** are unrelated. This issue is the general form of our **F9**.

title: fix(common)!: send the pagination wrapper in camelCase, as the schemas always said
body:
First of the 33 divergences #1076 recorded, and the one with the widest blast
radius per line changed.

## The bug

`Paginated<T>` (`vti-common/src/pagination/mod.rs`) carried no `rename_all`, so
every list task sent `next_cursor` and `total_estimate` against published
schemas that say `nextCursor` and `totalEstimate`.

A direct **R3.1** violation, and the same casing-drift class as #656/#658 —
which your own workspace guidance cites as how an empty `allowed_contexts`
silently minted a super-admin.

## Why nothing caught it

Three parties agreed with each other and none agreed with the contract:

- the service sent `next_cursor`
- `vtc-client`'s `Page<T>` mirrored **the service**, not the schema
- the admin SPA typed its fields from the service too

The module's own doc even documented `"next_cursor"` as the intended wire form.
The conformance witness from #1076 is what finally put implementation and
schema side by side.

Four consumers move together here. `audit.tsx` reads a `cursor` member of a
different shape and is deliberately untouched.

## The count goes 33 → 32, not 33 → 28

This is the part worth reading, and it corrects #1076's own module doc, which
claimed "5 entries, one fix".

Five entries cited the wrapper. **Only `relationships/list` becomes fully
conforming** — it was the only one whose drift was the wrapper *alone*, because
its spec types `items` as free objects. The other four also diverge at row
level (`createdByDid`, `vpClaims`, `MemberResponse` members), so they keep their
entries, rewritten to describe only what is left instead of restating a casing
bug that is now fixed.

**Closing a shared root cause moves four entries without closing them.** A count
that fell by five would have implied more progress than happened.

I did not work that out by reading — I tried 28, and
`known_drift_entries_still_diverge_where_they_say_they_do` refused it and named
the entries that still diverge. The guard earning its keep on its first real use
is a good sign for the remaining 32.

## Verified

- `cargo test -p vtc-service -p vti-common -p vtc-client` — 59 suites, 0 failures
- `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets -- -D warnings` — clean
- `cargo fmt --all --check` — clean
- `tsc -b --noEmit` in `admin-ui` — clean
- All three conformance tests pass at the corrected count

Branched from the #1077 hotfix and rebased onto merged main — deliberately not
cut from a main that would not compile.

## Breaking

`Paginated<T>` now serialises `nextCursor` / `totalEstimate`. `vti-common` is
published, so an external consumer reading the snake_case names breaks — though
what it was reading never matched the published schema. Every in-repo consumer
is updated in this PR.

## What is left, and the decision it needs

31 of the remaining 32 fall into two shapes. The larger is **no response
envelope** (12 entries): the spec wraps the payload and the handler returns the
bare object or array. Unlike this fix, that is twelve separate judgements about
whether the service or the spec is right, and it wants a stated default before
anyone starts — change the service to match the spec, or take the divergence
upstream where the service's shape is the better design.

title: Replace the four VID types with a declared correlation scope
body:
## Summary

The four VID types (R-DID, M-DID, C-DID, P-DID) each encode two independent
things in one name: **what the identifier is attached to**, and **how widely it
may be correlated**. Only the second is what implementers and users need to
reason about, and the first is already carried by the credential the identifier
appears in.

This proposes replacing the four types with a single declared property — the
scope over which an identifier may be correlated — and letting roles be
conferred by credentials, where they already are.

Raised as a follow-up to #21, which is a symptom of the same thing.

## The problem, concretely

The role axis is redundant with the credential type. A VMC's subject is a
member; a VRC's issuer is a party to a relationship. The credential says so.
Naming the identifier again duplicates that, and the duplication is where the
ambiguity lives, because the two can disagree.

Put an M-DID in a VRC — which §VRC explicitly permits — and both names apply.
Is it a membership DID or a relationship DID? The specification has to
disambiguate in prose, and that prose is #21.

The confusion is not hypothetical. In our implementation the word "persona" had
come to mean the membership DID, because a P-DID has no implementation and an
M-DID is described in the glossary as "a type of persona". An entire issue
(`OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure#1054`) was spent establishing which
identifier the specification was actually talking about.

## Proposal

One axis, monotonic from narrowest to widest, declared by the holder:

| Scope | Known to | Replaces |
|---|---|---|
| `pairwise` | exactly one counterparty | R-DID |
| `community` | one community | M-DID (not reused) |
| `linked` | a set the holder chooses | M-DID (reused), P-DID |
| `public` | unbounded, published, meant to be found | C-DID |

And the accompanying principle: **roles are conferred by credentials, scope is
declared by the holder.** An identifier is not "a membership DID"; it is an
identifier that *has* a membership credential. The VMC makes it a membership.
The name never did.

## What this buys

**The uniqueness requirement becomes definitional.** §Unilateral Relationship
Identification currently needs a normative MUST — "a new, unique R-DID for
every single entity they connect with" — plus a Privacy Consideration
explaining it. Under a scope axis, an identifier declared `pairwise` and used
with two counterparties simply is not pairwise. There is nothing left to
require.

**The public-community case stops being an anomaly.** A public open-source
community declares `community` or `public` and is done. No "bootstrapping", no
recommended migration, none of the framing problem raised in #21.

**C-DID stops being a special case.** A community's DID is a `public`-scoped
identifier that happens to be held by an organisation, not a fourth kind of
thing.

**Verifiers get the inference stated rather than implied.** Seeing `pairwise`
licenses exactly one conclusion: this identifier tells you nothing beyond this
relationship. That is the guarantee the whole model rests on, and today it is
only reachable by knowing what "R" stands for.

## Evidence from implementing it

We did not set out to propose this. Implementing pairwise publication in the
VTC forced an `IdentifierForm::{Attributed, Pairwise}` enum into existence,
because the code had to answer "how wide is this identifier claiming to be?"
and the four-type taxonomy does not answer that question — it answers a
different one. The community profile then needed a field declaring which form
the community expects, and the policy input needed to carry it.

A reference implementation independently reaching for a vocabulary the
specification does not have is the strongest evidence we can offer that the
vocabulary is missing.

## Where the four types are load-bearing, and should stay

Roles are not purely redundant. Two of them have real machinery:

- **Membership** is established by a VMC issued from a C-DID.
- **Persona** is asserted via a VPC.

Those mechanisms should stay exactly as they are. What should go is naming them
as *DID types*, which is the part that collides. Keeping the machinery and
dropping the type names costs nothing and removes the ambiguity.

## Costs, honestly

- It is a vocabulary change to a specification's core terms, which is more
  expensive than any fix in #21. Working Draft 01 is the cheapest moment it
  will ever be.
- R-DID / M-DID / C-DID / P-DID are established shorthand in this working
  group's conversation. They can survive as informal shorthand while the
  normative model uses scope — the same way people say "a web cert" without the
  specification defining that term.
- Declaring scope is not itself a correlation risk: the identifier *value* is
  what correlates. Declaring `pairwise` tells a verifier not to store it as a
  stable key, which helps.

## Requested

Whether the working group considers this in scope for WD02. We are willing to
write the specification text and to report back on what it takes to implement,
since we have already built the two-level version of it by accident.

title: VRC edge-verifiability conditions exist only in the glossary and contradict the body
body:
## Summary

The glossary definition of the VRC states conditions for edge verifiability that
appear nowhere in the body, contradict the body's Privacy Considerations, and
contradict the body's own bidirectional edge model. The VMC definition carries
half of the same construction.

The VRC entry (`spec/terms-definitions/verifiable_relationship_credential.md`)
has not been revised since the Working Draft 01 migration (#3), while the body's
treatment of R-DIDs, M-DIDs and the ZKP constructions has moved on. An
implementer reading the two together gets opposite instructions.

## Detail

The glossary entry reads:

> A VRC may contain either R-DIDs or M-DIDs. A VRC is only verifiable as a DTG
> edge in the context of a specific VTN if: a) it contains M-DIDs for both
> peers, b) both peers have signed the VRC using their M-DID private keys,
> c) both M-DIDs are verifiable via VMCs issued by VTCs, and d) those VTCs are
> recognized as VTN trust anchors in that VTN.

Three problems.

**1. It inverts the body's identifier guidance.** The body recommends the
opposite of condition (a):

- §VRC: "R-DIDs are RECOMMENDED for privacy; M-DIDs are allowed for
  bootstrapping (see Privacy Considerations)."
- §Unilateral Relationship Identification: "The valid application of this
  specification requires that each entity MUST generate a new, unique R-DID for
  every single entity they connect with, even within the same community."
- §Privacy Considerations 1: "Migration from M-DID-based to R-DID-based edges is
  recommended post-bootstrapping for enhanced privacy."

So the body tells an implementer to migrate to R-DID edges, and the glossary
tells the same implementer that an R-DID edge is not verifiable as an edge. Read
together, the privacy-preserving construction the body recommends is the one
that forfeits VTN-level edge verifiability.

**2. It is not reconciled with the Community-Anchored ZKP.** §Community-Anchored
Zero-Knowledge Proof states plainly that "Community membership is **not** a
precondition for issuing, holding, or presenting a VRC," and then defines a
construction in which the holder proves that "the VRC issuer possesses a VMC
from the *same* C-DID" *without revealing the specific DIDs*. That is the same
predicate the glossary's conditions (c) and (d) express by disclosure. If the
ZKP construction satisfies VTN-level edge verifiability, the glossary's
requirement for M-DIDs in the credential is unnecessary; if it does not, the
body should say so, because the ZKP section currently reads as though it does.
(Related: #9, on whether the linkages those constructions require are encoded at
all.)

**3. Condition (b) contradicts the bidirectional edge model** — and the first
sentence of the glossary entry itself. §VRC: "two VRCs (one each direction) form
a complete DTG edge," and the schema has a single `issuer` and a single `proof`.
The glossary entry opens by calling a VRC "one half of a bidirectional peer-to-
peer trust relationship" and then requires that "both peers have signed the VRC"
— which describes a single dual-signed credential, not two.

**4. The VMC entry carries the same unsourced construction.**
`verifiable_membership_credential.md`: "A VMC is only verifiable as a DTG edge in
the context of a specific VTN if the issuing VTC is recognized as a VTN trust
anchor on that VTN." Whether or not that one is correct, "only verifiable as a
DTG edge in the context of a specific VTN" is a normative-sounding constraint
that exists in no normative section. `grep` for it returns only these two
glossary files.

## Why it matters

This is not theoretical. In `OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure#1054` we are
deciding whether relationship credentials published to a community should carry
pairwise R-DIDs or membership M-DIDs, and the current VTC policy requires both
parties to be identifiable current members — which is the glossary's rule.
Choosing correctly requires knowing whether an R-DID edge is a first-class DTG
edge or a degraded one, and the specification currently answers both ways
depending on which file is read.

## Requested clarification

1. Is VTN-level edge verifiability intended to be a defined property of the
   specification at all? If so, it belongs in a normative section, not only in
   the glossary.
2. If it is: does a VRC carrying R-DIDs, presented with a community-anchored
   ZKP, satisfy it? Our reading of §Community-Anchored ZKP is that it should,
   and that condition (a) is a bootstrapping-era artifact.
3. Should condition (b) be struck as inconsistent with the two-VRC edge model,
   or does it describe an alternative single-credential form that the body does
   not define?
4. Should the VMC entry's edge-verifiability sentence be moved to the body or
   removed?

Happy to open a PR against `spec/terms-definitions/` and the relevant body
sections once the group has a view on (1) and (2) — the answer to (2) in
particular changes what the fix looks like rather than just where it lands.

title: Relationship policy discovery: both communities must admit an edge, neither can find out
body:
## Summary

Forming an edge between two communities requires **both** communities' policies
to admit it, and there is no way for either side to learn the other's policy
before trying. The first signal that an edge is inadmissible is a rejection,
after one half has already been published.

Raising this as an interoperability question rather than a purely local one: the
failure is symmetric and neither party can fix it alone, which is the shape of
thing a specification usually settles.

## Detail

A cross-community edge needs two independent permissions:

- The **public** community must accept a half whose subject is an opaque
  pairwise identifier belonging to a non-member.
- The **private** community must permit its member to name an outsider in a
  credential at all.

Each is a reasonable policy position, and either may be "no". Nothing published
by either community says which.

A concrete instance from our implementation. Our default relationship policy has
two branches:

```rego
# Pairwise: membership comes from the session.
allow if {
    input.action == "publish"
    input.authenticated_member.is_current
    input.identifier_form == "pairwise"
}

# Attributed: both named parties are community members.
allow if {
    input.action == "publish"
    input.identifier_form == "attributed"
    input.issuer.is_current
    input.subject.is_current
}
```

The public member's half is *attributed* — that is the whole point of a public
community — and its subject is an outsider, so `input.subject.is_current` is
false and the publish is denied. The pairwise branch would admit an opaque
subject, but only when the publisher's own identifier is pairwise, which is
exactly what the public community has declared it does not use.

So the edge fails, correctly, under a policy that is defensible on its own
terms. What is missing is any way for the other party to have known that before
publishing their half — and by then the private member has already issued a
credential naming someone who cannot reciprocate.

## Why it matters

Both parties behave conformantly and the edge still fails, which makes this an
interoperability property rather than a local configuration choice. It also
fails asymmetrically in time: whichever party publishes first has already
disclosed something.

The information needed is small — whether a community accepts non-member
subjects, and which identifier forms it will publish under. Those are properties
a community can state without revealing anything about its membership, which
matters because the communities most likely to refuse are the private ones.

## Requested clarification

1. Should a community publish enough of its relationship policy for a
   counterparty to determine, before publishing, whether an edge is admissible?
2. If so, is that a discoverable field on the community profile, and is it in
   scope for this specification or for the Trust Task layer?
3. Is there an intended ordering for edge formation that avoids one party
   disclosing before the other's admissibility is known?

**Proposed answer**: publish the relevant predicates — accepted subject forms,
accepted issuer identifier forms — as a discoverable field on the community
profile. It is cheap, it reveals nothing about membership, and it turns a failed
publish into a pre-flight check. We will implement this locally either way; the
question for the group is whether it should be interoperable, since a
locally-invented field helps nobody else.

## Context

Raised while implementing the VRC path in
`OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure`. Set out as item X4 in the
["Across communities" section of the DTG conformance
review](https://docs.fpp.storm.ws/dtg-conformance-infographic.html). Related:
#21, #22, and the two companion cross-community questions filed alongside this
one.

title: Edge verifiability across VTN contexts: different VTNs, or none at all
body:
## Summary

The VRC and VMC glossary entries make edge verifiability conditional on the
issuing VTCs being recognized as trust anchors *in a specific VTN*. Neither
entry says what happens when the two peers' VTCs anchor in **different** VTNs,
or when one anchors in **none** — which is the deliberate posture of a private
community. The condition is silent on precisely the case a spanning layer exists
to serve.

This is the fourth question in #21 seen from the cross-community direction. It
is filed separately because #21 asks whether the condition should exist at all,
while this asks what it means if it survives.

## Detail

The VRC entry (`spec/terms-definitions/verifiable_relationship_credential.md`):

> A VRC is only verifiable as a DTG edge in the context of a specific VTN if:
> a) it contains M-DIDs for both peers, b) both peers have signed the VRC using
> their M-DID private keys, c) both M-DIDs are verifiable via VMCs issued by
> VTCs, and d) **those VTCs are recognized as VTN trust anchors in that VTN**.

The VMC entry carries the same construction in one clause.

Condition (d) is stated as though one VTN context governs the whole edge. Three
cases it does not cover:

**1. The two VTCs anchor in different VTNs.** Each half traces to a VTC that
some VTN recognises, but no single VTN recognises both. Is the edge verifiable
in either context? In neither? The text gives no rule, and the natural readings
disagree — "in the context of a specific VTN" could mean *the verifier's* VTN or
*an* agreed VTN, and those produce different answers.

**2. One peer's VTC anchors in no VTN, deliberately.** A community that exists
precisely so its membership is not discoverable has no reason to seek anchor
status anywhere. Under condition (d) every edge it forms with the outside world
is, permanently and by construction, not a verifiable DTG edge — not because
anything is unproven, but because a party chose privacy.

**3. The verifier is outside both.** An external verifier can check that both
halves are authentic and that each traces to *some* VTC. Condition (d) does not
let it conclude anything, because it asks about recognition rather than about
what the verifier can check.

## Why it matters

Under condition (d) as written, verifiability is a property of the *network the
issuers joined*, not of what a verifier can establish. Two edges with identical
cryptography and identical proofs get different answers depending on registry
membership neither peer controls at verification time.

The cross-community case is where the spanning layer earns its name. If an edge
between two communities can never be a verifiable DTG edge unless both
communities' VTCs happen to anchor in the same VTN, then the answer for the
motivating case is "no", and that should be stated deliberately rather than
arrived at by silence.

## Requested clarification

1. For an edge whose peers' VTCs anchor in different VTNs, which VTN's context
   governs?
2. Is an edge with one deliberately unanchored peer intended to be permanently
   unverifiable as a DTG edge?
3. Should edge verifiability be defined **per verifier** — what this verifier
   can establish — rather than per VTN?

**Proposed answer**: resolve alongside #21 Q1 and Q2. If edge verifiability
survives as a defined property, define it per verifier and in terms of what must
be checkable, not which registry the issuers appear in. A verifier that trusts
both VTCs by any route should reach the same conclusion whether or not a VTN
mediated that trust.

## Context

Raised while implementing the VRC path in
`OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure`. Set out as item X3 in the
["Across communities" section of the DTG conformance
review](https://docs.fpp.storm.ws/dtg-conformance-infographic.html). Directly
dependent on #21; related to #22.

title: Name the asymmetric edge: two halves may declare different correlation scopes
body:
## Summary

The specification assumes both halves of a DTG edge are the same kind of thing.
When two communities with opposite disclosure policies form an edge, they are
not: one half is published under an attributed, correlatable identifier and the
other under a pairwise one. The four VID types cannot name this edge, and
nothing states what an implementation should conclude about its privacy.

This is not the mixed-scope community case (a community that uses different
identifier kinds internally). It is two communities, two policies, and one edge
whose halves legitimately disagree.

## Detail

A DTG edge is two VRCs, one in each direction. Each party issues its own half
and chooses the identifier it appears under. Neither can impose that choice on
the other, and neither needs to.

Take a deliberately public community — an open-source project whose whole value
is that contributions trace back to named people — and a deliberately private
one, where members are known to each other only by per-counterparty identifiers.
A member of each forms a relationship with a member of the other:

- Half 1 is issued by the public member under an attributed identifier, into a
  graph anyone can read.
- Half 2 is issued by the private member under an R-DID that only their
  counterparty can map to them.

Both halves are conformant. The edge is one edge.

**1. The taxonomy has no word for it.** Under the four VID types, an implementer
must ask whether this is an R-DID edge or an M-DID edge. It is one of each.
There is no answer, because the question presumes both halves are the same kind.
This is a stronger argument for the structural change proposed in #22 than the
mixed-scope community case is: there, one authority chooses; here, no single
party is entitled to choose.

**2. Nothing says an edge's effective privacy is the minimum of its halves.**
The private member declared the scope of *their own* identifier, and that
declaration is honoured — only their counterparty can resolve it. But their
counterparty publishes the other half into a public, correlatable graph, so the
pairwise identifier now sits next to a named person in a place anyone can read.

The private member has no say in where the other half is published, and no way
to discover it. §Privacy Considerations 2 addresses R-DID uniqueness — reuse
across counterparties — which is a different failure. Nothing addresses the case
where a *correctly unique* R-DID is correlated by what the other party does with
its own half.

The rule that seems to be missing: **an edge's effective disclosure is the
maximum of its two halves; a declared scope binds only its own holder.** Neither
sentence appears in the specification, and an implementation that computed
privacy from one half alone would be wrong in a way nothing warns it about.

## Why it matters

Cross-community edges are the interesting case for a trust spanning layer — an
edge inside one community is governed by one policy and needs no reconciliation.
If the specification only describes edges whose halves agree, it describes the
case that does not need it.

An implementation reading the current text will reasonably conclude that a
pairwise-declared identifier stays pairwise. In the cross-community case it does
not, and the party who loses privacy is the one who followed the guidance.

## Requested clarification

1. Does the specification acknowledge that the two halves of one edge may
   declare different scopes, and is that a conformant edge?
2. Should it state that a declared scope constrains only its own holder's
   disclosure, and that an edge's effective disclosure is the maximum of its
   halves?
3. Should that appear as a Privacy Consideration, or normatively?

**Proposed answer**, for the group to react to rather than open cold: name it.
State that scope is declared per identifier and experienced per edge, that
halves may legitimately differ, and add the maximum rule as a Privacy
Consideration. Under the declared-scope model in #22 this falls out of the
vocabulary; under the four types it needs prose.

## Context

Raised while implementing the VRC path in
`OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure`. The cross-community analysis is set
out in full, with the graph drawn from a single shared edge list, in the
["Across communities" section of the DTG conformance
review](https://docs.fpp.storm.ws/dtg-conformance-infographic.html) (items
X1 and X2). Related: #21 (edge verifiability), #22 (declared correlation
scope).

title: fix(common)!: send the pagination wrapper in camelCase, as the schemas always said (#1078)
body:
fix(common)!: send the pagination wrapper in camelCase, as the schemas always said (#1078)

`Paginated<T>` carried no `rename_all`, so every list task sent `next_cursor`
and `total_estimate` against published schemas that say `nextCursor` and
`totalEstimate`. A direct R3.1 violation, and the same casing-drift class as
#656/#658 — where an empty `allowed_contexts` silently minted a super-admin.

Nothing caught it because nothing compared the two. The service sent one
spelling, `vtc-client` mirrored the service rather than the schema, and the
admin SPA typed its fields from the service too. All three agreed with each
other and none agreed with the contract. The conformance witness added in
#1076 is what finally put them side by side.

Four consumers move together: the wrapper in `vti-common`, `vtc-client`'s
`Page<T>`, and the `joinRequests` and `members` admin plugins. `audit.tsx`
reads a `cursor` member of a different shape and is untouched.

## The count goes 33 → 32, not 33 → 28

The witness refused 28 and accepted 32, which is the useful part of this
change and the reason the module doc is rewritten rather than decremented.

Five entries cited the wrapper. Only `relationships/list` becomes fully
conforming, because it was the only one whose drift was the wrapper alone —
its spec types `items` as free objects. The other four still diverge at row
level (`createdByDid`, `vpClaims`, `MemberResponse` members) and keep their
entries, now describing only what is left rather than restating a casing bug
that is fixed.

Closing a shared root cause moves four entries without closing them. A drift
count that fell by five would have implied more progress than happened, and
`known_drift_entries_still_diverge_where_they_say_they_do` is what stopped it
saying so.

BREAKING CHANGE: `Paginated<T>` serialises `nextCursor` / `totalEstimate`
instead of `next_cursor` / `total_estimate`. `vti-common` is published, so any
external consumer reading the snake_case names breaks — they were reading
something that never matched the published schema. Every in-repo consumer is
updated here.

Refs #1059

title: fix(vtc): thread `now` into the VPC shape check, unbreaking main
body:
**`main` at `397d087c` does not compile.** This unbreaks it.

```
error[E0061]: this function takes 4 arguments but 3 arguments were supplied
   --> vtc-service/src/routes/relationships.rs:994
```

## How three green PRs produced a red main

#1074 added `check_vpc_shape`, which calls `credentials::ingress::require_dtg_type`.
#1075 gave that function a `now` parameter.

Neither diff touched the other's lines, so git merged both cleanly and **both were green on CI** — each having been tested against a `main` that did not yet contain the other. A textual merge and a semantic conflict.

Nothing in the repo would have caught it. CI green on a pull request proves the branch works against the main it was *cut from*, not the main it will *land on*.

## The fix, and the decision inside it

`check_vpc_shape` now takes `now` and threads it through, matching `check_vrc_shape` beside it.

That is not only what the compiler wanted. It answers a question neither PR was positioned to ask: **should a VPC's validity window be checked when it is attached?** It should, for the same reason the window is checked on the publish path — an annotation that outlived its own credential would go on asserting a persona the issuer had stopped standing behind. `now` is read once per request and passed in, so every check in the request evaluates at one instant.

Had this been resolved as a pure compiler fixup, the obvious move would have been to pass a `now` that skips the check. That would have compiled and been wrong.

## Verified

Cut from `397d087c`, so this is against **all three** of #1074, #1075 and #1076 together.

- `cargo check -p vtc-service` — compiles
- `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets -- -D warnings` — clean
- `cargo fmt --all --check` — clean
- #1076's conformance witness passes on the fixed tree, including `known_drift_entries_still_diverge_where_they_say_they_do`

The full `cargo test -p vtc-service` run was at 51 suites / 0 failures when this PR was opened, and was not waited out — main being red is the more urgent fact, and a full re-test is planned once this lands.

## Worth acting on separately

Two changes to one function signature need one rebased onto the other before either merges, however disjoint their diffs look. A merge queue, or requiring branches to be current before merge, would enforce that mechanically. This PR does not add either — flagging it rather than bundling it.

title: test(vtc): witness that every bound Trust Task speaks its published schema
body:
Closes #1059.

The VTC binds 58 published `spec/vtc/*` Trust Task URIs and nothing checked
that any of them speaks its URI's wire shape. The two parity checks in
`vtc-service/tests/trust_task_manifest.rs` are about identity — the URI
resolves in `trust_tasks_rs::schema_index` — not shape, and there is no
runtime validation on this side either: the document dispatcher's
`parse_payload` (`vtc-service/src/trust_tasks/helpers.rs:59`) is a bare
`serde_json::from_value`, and the REST layer's gate checks the `Trust-Task`
header, not the body. So a response could diverge arbitrarily from the schema
its URI names and every gate stayed green.

This ports `vta-service/src/trust_tasks/conformance.rs` (#857), following its
shape rather than inventing a second idiom for the same job: a derived census,
a witness table, mechanical non-vacuity.

## What it does

`vtc-service/src/trust_tasks/conformance.rs`, a `#[cfg(test)]` module in `src`
because its census needs `DISPATCHED_URIS`, which no integration test can see.

- The census is derived from both places this service binds a task: the REST
  tower layers in `routes/mod.rs`, read as source text because a built axum
  `Router` cannot be enumerated for them (the technique
  `tests/trust_task_manifest.rs` already uses), and `DISPATCHED_URIS`, the
  document dispatcher's own list. Union, filtered to what `schema_for`
  resolves.
- Every URI in it must have a `checked!` witness or an annotated `drift!`
  entry, asserted in both directions — a URI with no witness and a witness for
  a URI nothing binds both fail.
- Both sides of each witness are parsed as the generated `Payload` /
  `Response` and validated against the embedded schema. Schema validation is
  not redundant with parsing: serde ignores `const`, `enum`, `pattern` and
  `minLength` entirely, and `submit/0.1`'s response `status` is a
  `const: "pending"` that no generated struct enforces. It caught two of my
  own fixtures during development — a truncated `vrcSha256` that serde
  accepted and `^[0-9a-f]{64}$` did not.

  sweep, which validates the request only. The VTA's note ("the codegen emits
  `ValidatedPayload` for `Payload` but not for `Response`") was true of the
  0.4/0.5 codegen and is stale at the 0.11 series this workspace pins.
