title: Trust Task Context Binding on published mechanisms, taskContext re-anchoring, and W3C proof/digest alignment
body:
Consolidated Working Draft 01 batch from the task force's working fork, superseding #15 by carrying it: the first commits are @bmiller59's #15 restructuring (authorship preserved), with three further changes built on top of it and the #15 first-pass review addressed. Closes #11. Resolves #17.

## What's inside, in order

**1. The #15 restructuring** (@bmiller59) — Trust Task Context Binding depends only on mechanisms already defined in the Trust Tasks core specification; the "qualifying specification" profile; outcome evidence travels with the presentation.

**2. `taskContext` re-anchoring and framework-0.4 alignment** — the outcome of trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf#173: `taskContext` carries the **`id` of the originating exchange's initiating document** (globally unique per the core specification's §4.3; the innermost exchange that attests the event, per §4.9.1), retiring the issuer-side uniqueness workaround. The qualifying profile is reworded against framework 0.4 (per-variant proof; the error variant honestly excluded — a task specification cannot strengthen `trust-task-error`'s own declaration; the no-`#response` escape hatch dropped). Outcome Interpretability cites the core specification's reply-disposition classification (§8.6) rather than hand-rolling the terminal/non-terminal split, and states the verifier's pairing checklist for retained evidence. A `trust-task-error` is failure evidence only, attributable to third parties when it carries `inResponseTo` (§8.2).

**3. W3C proof and digest alignment** (#17, all three items) — the VWC digest becomes `digestMultibase` (multibase multihash over the JCS canonical form the definition already named); multibase headers restricted to `z`/`u` per CID 1.0 §2.4 with alphabets enforced; proofs move from `Ed25519Signature2020` to the `DataIntegrityProof` envelope with `eddsa-jcs-2022` as the RECOMMENDED default suite (offline-verifiable; one canonicalization shared with `digestMultibase`) and `bbs-2023` named as the selective-disclosure path.

**4. The #15 first-pass review, addressed** — normative citations are commit-pinned permalinks (framework 0.4, `fbe196a`) so "pinned" is literally true; the stray subsection marking is removed; the per-issuer-uniqueness comment is mooted by the re-anchoring; and the term **"Trust Tasks core specification"** is now defined (`spec/terms-definitions/`), stating the core-vs-individual-specification architecture, explaining the upstream document's own "framework 0.4" version labels, and explicitly disclaiming the ToIP governance-framework sense.

## Evidence

The pairing checklist and the anchoring rule are executable: [`tsp-reference/ref-06w-witnessed-exchange`](https://github.com/berkmancenter/keyring-wallet/tree/doc/tsp-plan/tsp-reference/ref-06w-witnessed-exchange) runs the witnessed exchange end-to-end — the VWC's `taskContext` lands on the ceremony's initiating document `id` structurally, and the retained `submit#response` passes exactly the checks the text states. The digest change is encoding-only for implementations already canonicalizing with JCS (verified against the Keyring witness implementation's own digest function).

Spec-Up-T render verified locally: every `[[ref:]]` resolves, no unresolved terms. Review history: Mickens-Lab/dtgwg-cred-spec#2, Mickens-Lab/dtgwg-cred-spec#3, Mickens-Lab/dtgwg-cred-spec#4.

title: Idempotency keys for consequential VTA Trust Tasks, and a defined retry owner per failure domain
body:
Surfaced by an external RAHP/DRARM assessment of the OpenVTC Cypress release
(sankarshanmukhopadhyay/rahp-toolkit#18, finding `OVTC-RAHP-01`). The
assessment filed it against the OpenVTC client, but the fix belongs here: a
client cannot make a server-side mutation idempotent on its own.

This overlaps with, and generalises, remediation-plan item **F3**
(`vta-service/src/operations/provision_integration/mod.rs:343`) and is the
enforcement mechanism for stack development guide rule **R1.4**.

## Problem

Consequential VTA Trust Tasks carry no idempotency or correlation key that the
server dedups on. Any client that retries a timed-out request — correctly, on a
transport fault where the request most likely never arrived — can produce a
duplicate durable effect when the request *did* arrive and only the reply was
lost.

OpenVTC's `vta_retry` is a well-behaved caller: bounded at 3 attempts, backed
off, and retrying only transport/timeout/5xx faults
(`openvtc/src/state_handler/setup_sequence/vta.rs:38-73`). It is still exposed,
because the safety property is not available to it.

Two aggravating factors:

**1. Auto-assigned paths turn a detectable duplicate into a silent orphan.**
OpenVTC only ever calls `create_did_webvh` with `WebvhPathMode::AutoAssign`
(`create_persona.rs:66`, `join_flow.rs:1002`). With an explicit path, a retried
create collides and the server returns Conflict — visible, recoverable. With
AutoAssign, the retry receives a *different* path, so the first DID is published
in the webvh log with nobody holding a reference to it. The client never learns
it exists.

**2. Retry layers compose.** The TDK delivery layer already retries
independently — durable outbox with exponential backoff
(`affinidi-messaging-delivery/src/drain.rs`, `confirm.rs`) — underneath
application-level retry. The delivery layer dedups at the receiver; VTA Trust
Tasks do not, so attempts multiply across layers with no dedup at the point
where the durable effect lands.

## Proposed change

1. **Classify every Trust Task** as read-only, naturally idempotent,
   idempotency-keyed, or unsafe-to-retry. Publish the classification alongside
   the task definitions so clients can reason about retry safety without reading
   the server.
2. **Accept a client-supplied idempotency key** on consequential mutations —
   `create_key`, `create_did_webvh`, `delete_did_webvh`, and the
   provision-integration flow (F3) at minimum. Same key + same request →
   the original result, not a second effect. Same key + different request →
   an explicit conflict error, not silent acceptance of either.
3. **Retention window** for the dedup record long enough to cover realistic
   client retry budgets plus a lost-reply gap; document it, since it is part of
   the contract.
4. **Define retry ownership per failure domain** so delivery-layer, SDK, and
   application retries cannot multiply attempts independently. State which layer
   owns retry for Trust Tasks and make the others pass through.
5. **Server retry hints.** Honour and cap `Retry-After` on the client side
   (DRARM `RLA-029`, currently a review-required gap in the assessment).
6. **Reconciliation for what already exists.** An orphaned auto-assigned
   `did:webvh` is inert but published. A sweeper or a
   list-context-DIDs-and-compare path would let operators find and retire them.

## Acceptance

- A lost-reply test: the same create request replayed with the same idempotency
  key converges to one logical effect, verified in the webvh log and in
  keyspace state.
- The same for delete, and for provision-integration (closing F3).
- Mismatched-body reuse of a key is rejected explicitly.
- Retry ownership is documented and the redundant layers are demonstrably
  pass-through.

## Notes

Severity: we assess this Medium rather than the assessment's High/potentially
Critical. The failure produces a rare inert orphan, not a crossed security
boundary or a double effect on live state — but it is durable, published, and
invisible to the party responsible for it, which is why it is worth closing
properly rather than documenting as accepted risk.

title: fix(service)!: make AppState non-exhaustive so adding a field stops being a break
body:
## The problem

`AppState` is **46 public fields, zero private fields, no constructor guard**.
Before this, any crate could write an `AppState { .. }` literal — which makes
*adding a field* a source-breaking change under
`constructible_struct_adds_field`.

Twenty-nine commits have added at least one field to it. `c93c7b57` added five
in one go.

**That break has never once been reported.** `cargo semver-checks` cannot build
this crate's baseline, and a crate whose baseline fails to build is silently not
compared — indistinguishable from a crate that was compared and found clean.
(That baseline failure turned out to be a real defect in the published crate,
not a tooling artifact; it is being handled separately.)

## Why the version numbers were right anyway

They were, and it is worth recording *why*, because the reason is two
coincidences rather than a process:

1. At `0.x` a breaking change needs a **minor** bump, and conventional commits
   already force a minor for `feat:`.
2. Every field addition since release-plz adoption happened to be a `feat:`.

So the correct bump was demanded by commit classification, not by the semver
check — which never ran. Something was incidentally standing where the dead
check stood.

**Neither coincidence holds in general:**

| | |
|---|---|
| `refactor:` / `fix:` / `perf:` / `chore:` | all yield a **patch**, all can add fields |
| `c93c7b57` | a `refactor:` that added **five** fields — the largest single addition in the file's history |
| at 1.0 | a break needs a **major**, `feat:` gives only a minor — the alignment fails entirely |

Moving state between structs is what a refactor *is*, so the commit type most
likely to add public fields is one of the types that yields a patch. That is a
structural pairing, not bad luck. And the cover expires precisely when the
consequences become external.

`#[non_exhaustive]` closes the class permanently rather than relying on any of
that continuing to hold.

## Why this is safe

Nothing outside the crate is affected:

- both construction sites are in-crate — `build_app_state` and `test_support`
- `MockVta` is the supported entry point for external consumers
- `tests/app_state_single_construction.rs` already goes through
  `build_app_state` rather than a literal

That last one matters: the test is from the **P1.1 work in `c93c7b57`** — the
same commit that added five fields. A single canonical constructor was already
the crate's intent. This makes it enforceable from outside rather than
conventional.

## The `!`

Marked breaking because it is: outside this crate, `AppState { .. }` and
exhaustive destructuring stop compiling. **That is the point.** It is one final
break, and it is the last one this struct can have.

## Verification

- `cargo test --workspace` — 145 suites, 0 failed
- `cargo check -p vta-service --all-features` — clean, zero warnings

## Checklist (stack guide §9)

- [x] No new `reqwest::Client::new()` / bare `fetch()` (R1.2)
- [x] No lock held across a network await (R1.3)
- [x] No local state committed before its remote effect (R2.1)
- [x] Every retry bounded + backed off (R1.4)
- [x] Accept/poll/listen loops survive transient errors (R1.5)
- [x] Acks/deletes happen only after durable handoff (R1.6)
- [x] New/changed wire types (R3.*) — none; this is a Rust source-level
      constructibility change with no wire effect
- [x] Config absence = most restrictive (R5.*)
- [x] **Logs/status claim only what was verified (R6.\*)** — the doc comment
      states the version numbers were correct and says plainly that this was
      coincidence, rather than implying the check was working

title: fix(rebuild): store membership credentials at the VTA, and query the vault legally
body:
## Why

**Membership recovery restored nothing.** Running #250 against a live VTA found three defects — all in assumptions about the credential vault's *contract* rather than in the code, which is why the unit tests could not catch them: they feed the plan a listing of full credential bodies, a fair model of the design and wrong about the service.

Two of these shipped in #248 and #250. This is a fix against `main`.

## The three defects

**1. A `MembershipCredential` was never stored at the VTA at all.** Invitations were pushed to the credential vault on receipt; VMCs went into the local `CommunityRecord` and nowhere else. `rebuild` reconstructs a membership *from* its credential — the right design, since the credential is what the community signed and it names both parties — but the credential has to be somewhere other than the config file a rebuild exists *because you no longer have*.

**2. `cred_vault_query({})` is refused by design.** The vault is deliberately non-enumerable — `CredentialQuery::is_empty()` exists precisely to reject a filterless request, because *"running it would be a wallet enumeration"*. Both `rebuild` and `context_probe` sent `{}`, and **both read the refusal as "zero credentials" and carried on**. So the occupied-context probe was under-reporting too.

**3. `query/0.1` returns body-free descriptors** — `id`, `types`, `issuerDid`, `purpose`, `status`. A membership is defined by its **subject**, which only the body carries, so every descriptor would have been rejected as `NoSubject`. Each is now fetched with `get/0.1` before verification.

## Published Trust Tasks only

Every call dispatches through `dispatch_trust_task`:

- `spec/vault/credentials/receive/0.1` — store
- `spec/vault/credentials/query/0.1` — find, **filtered**
- `spec/vault/credentials/get/0.1` — fetch a body

No bespoke routes.

## Design notes

**The sync runs on connect**, not at message ingest, because the dispatch path has no VTA session. One mechanism then covers three cases: a join that just completed, a credential received while the VTA was unreachable, and the back-fill of every membership from before this existed. It's idempotent — the vault keys a received credential on the VC's own `id` — so the query pass exists only to avoid pointless writes on every launch.

**The probe no longer counts credentials.** Non-enumeration is the point, so "how many credentials are here?" is a question the contract doesn't answer. Personas and sub-contexts are enough to tell a context is in use, and both are properly enumerable.

**Both query filters are factored into named functions** so a test can assert they carry a filter. A future edit that drops one fails in CI rather than in production, silently restoring nothing.

## `openvtc health --recoverable`

The read-only diagnostic that found all of this, kept because *"if this machine were lost, could this account be rebuilt?"* is worth being able to ask at any time. It runs the same plan the wizard's Recover option would and prints it instead of applying it.

It reports credentials held **locally** alongside those held **at the VTA** — without that a reader cannot tell "no memberships" from "not stored at the VTA yet", and those need different actions.

## Verified end to end against a live VTA

Before:
```
  held locally     1 membership credential(s)
  would restore    1 persona, 0 memberships
  ⚠ 1 membership credential(s) are held locally but not at the VTA…
```

After:
```
  at the VTA       1 persona, 1 membership
  held locally     1 membership credential(s)
  would restore    1 persona, 1 membership
  RECOVERABLE: every identity in this context maps to its keys.
```

Stored via `receive`, found via filtered `query`, body fetched via `get`, verified against the persona. The key mapping (`select_secret_kid`) was also confirmed working — 24 keys present, correctly attributed, none mis-assigned.

Full gate green: fmt, clippy `-D warnings`, both test configurations, and `cargo doc -D warnings`.

title: vta-service-v0.18.0
body:
### Added

- **service**: Retire an orphaned webvh slot, on evidence rather than assertion ([#1022](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/pull/1022))

`vta/webvh/servers/reconcile` names two divergences and repairs
  neither, deliberately — they want opposite remedies. This implements the
  remedy for one: the orphan, a slot a hosting server serves for this VTA
  that the VTA has no record of.

  Nothing could repair that state, and the reason is structural. Every
  delete addresses a DID through its local record, which is what says
  which server to talk to and which keys to sign with; an orphan is
  defined by that record's absence, so the lookup fails before a request
  leaves the VTA. Nor can the caller go around it — the VTA holds the host
  credentials. A slot both parties can see, and neither can remove.

- **service**: The vta/services task family, and the twenty routes it supersedes ([#1017](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/pull/1017))

* feat(service): the vta/services task family, one verb per task

  Eight handlers covering what twenty `/services/*` REST routes did. The
  operations are untouched — `operations::protocol::*` already implements each
  transport — so this is the parameterised door onto them, not new logic.

  `service` names the transport and `config` carries its settings, so the fan-out
  happens here rather than on the wire. That is what keeps a fifth transport to a
  config variant instead of four new specs.

  **The drain guard is the part that matters.** Tearing down a mediator discards
  whatever is in flight through it, so `disable`/`update`/`rollback` on didcomm
  pass a `DisableTransport` that decides whether the 1-hour floor applies. The
  REST route hardcodes `Rest` and the DIDComm handler hardcodes `Didcomm`,
  because each IS that path; a trust task is not, so it reads the arrival
  transport from the dispatch spine.

  The spine records confidentiality, not binding: DIDComm and TSP are both
  `EndToEnd` and it cannot tell them apart. `EndToEnd` therefore maps to
  `Didcomm`, which OVER-applies the floor to a TSP-carried disable that does not
  strictly need it. Deliberate: under-applying tears down the mediator a request
  arrived through and discards the reply to the very task asking for it, while
  over-applying only delays a teardown the operator can repeat. The ambiguous
  case takes the cheaper mistake.

  Three shapes the generated types forced, each documented where it lands:

  - `ServiceMutationResult` and `RollbackKind` are duplicated per family —
    identical shapes, distinct types. Mutation results round-trip through the wire
    form rather than being hand-copied three times; rollback kinds go through a
    macro that names the variants, so a divergence is a compile error.
  - Rollback may write nothing. Its `noOp` arm has no `logEntryVersionId`, which
    is why it has its own result type, and the witness uses exactly that arm.
  - `handshake_timeout_secs` is `NonZeroU64` — the schema's `minimum: 1` — so the
    default is constructed, not unwrapped.

  **Operation futures are boxed, and that is load-bearing.** These handlers fan
  out to four sizeable futures, awaited inside a dispatch match that already
  carries every other task's state machine. Inlining them grew the frame past the
  default 8 MiB stack and aborted an unrelated mock_vta test with a stack
  overflow — which reads as infinite recursion and is not.

- **vta**: Dedup keyed Trust Tasks on an idempotency key ([#1011](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/pull/1011))

A client that retries a timed-out request is doing the right thing. The
  dangerous case is the one where the VTA processed it and only the reply
  was lost, because the retry then produces a second durable effect —
  `webvh/dids/create` being the sharp example, where auto-assigned paths
  mean the retry mints a *different* DID and the first stays published
  with nobody holding a reference to it.

  The existing `trust_tasks::replay` layer cannot catch that. It keys on
  `(actor, envelope-id)` and every SDK path mints a fresh `urn:uuid:` per
  attempt, so a genuine retry sails past it. Its own module docs name this
  work as the deliberate follow-up.

title: vta-tee-v0.1.9
body:
### Fixed

- **tee**: Bootstrap 410 and vsock enotconn ([#1003](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/pull/1003))

* fix(tee): retry transient ENOTCONN on first vsock config-overlay read

  tokio-vsock can report a stream connected just before Nitro finishes the
  nonblocking handshake, so the very first read on a fresh vsock:5800
  connection to the parent config server can return ENOTCONN even though
  the parent is listening and ready. Retry only that specific transient
  error kind with a short delay; any other I/O error still fails closed
  immediately, and the existing overall READ_TIMEOUT deadline still
  bounds the whole fetch.

  Adds positive (retries ENOTCONN then succeeds) and negative (does not
  retry PermissionDenied) unit tests against the inner read loop.

title: pnm-cli-v0.12.8
body:
### Documentation

- **pnm-cli**: Document the tsp and azure-secrets build features ([#1016](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/pull/1016))

The README's Feature Flags table listed two of the crate's four features.
  Both omissions changed what an operator ends up with:

  `tsp` is a default (`default = ["keyring", "tsp"]`) and gates the round-trip
  TSP probe in `pnm health`. The keyring-free build the README recommended,
  `--no-default-features --features config-session`, silently dropped it, after
  which `pnm health` reports an advertised TSPTransport service without ever
  exercising it. The build examples now re-add `tsp` and say why.

  `azure-secrets` is off by default and inert unless `keyring` is also off --
  the backend's Azure arm is gated `not(feature = "keyring")` -- so adding it to
  a default build selects nothing and reports no error.

  The section also claimed "at least one of keyring or config-session must be
  enabled". Nothing enforces that. With neither, the backend falls through to
  the plaintext file store and warns on every access, which is a materially
  different guarantee from the build-time gate the sentence implied. Replaced
  with the real selection order, keyring -> azure-secrets -> config-session ->
  plaintext fallback, and the warning verbatim.

body:
### Added

- **service**: Retire an orphaned webvh slot, on evidence rather than assertion ([#1022](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/pull/1022))

`vta/webvh/servers/reconcile` names two divergences and repairs
  neither, deliberately — they want opposite remedies. This implements the
  remedy for one: the orphan, a slot a hosting server serves for this VTA
  that the VTA has no record of.

  Nothing could repair that state, and the reason is structural. Every
  delete addresses a DID through its local record, which is what says
  which server to talk to and which keys to sign with; an orphan is
  defined by that record's absence, so the lookup fails before a request
  leaves the VTA. Nor can the caller go around it — the VTA holds the host
  credentials. A slot both parties can see, and neither can remove.

- **service**: The vta/services task family, and the twenty routes it supersedes ([#1017](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/pull/1017))

* feat(service): the vta/services task family, one verb per task

  Eight handlers covering what twenty `/services/*` REST routes did. The
  operations are untouched — `operations::protocol::*` already implements each
  transport — so this is the parameterised door onto them, not new logic.

  `service` names the transport and `config` carries its settings, so the fan-out
  happens here rather than on the wire. That is what keeps a fifth transport to a
  config variant instead of four new specs.

  **The drain guard is the part that matters.** Tearing down a mediator discards
  whatever is in flight through it, so `disable`/`update`/`rollback` on didcomm
  pass a `DisableTransport` that decides whether the 1-hour floor applies. The
  REST route hardcodes `Rest` and the DIDComm handler hardcodes `Didcomm`,
  because each IS that path; a trust task is not, so it reads the arrival
  transport from the dispatch spine.

  The spine records confidentiality, not binding: DIDComm and TSP are both
  `EndToEnd` and it cannot tell them apart. `EndToEnd` therefore maps to
  `Didcomm`, which OVER-applies the floor to a TSP-carried disable that does not
  strictly need it. Deliberate: under-applying tears down the mediator a request
  arrived through and discards the reply to the very task asking for it, while
  over-applying only delays a teardown the operator can repeat. The ambiguous
  case takes the cheaper mistake.

  Three shapes the generated types forced, each documented where it lands:

  - `ServiceMutationResult` and `RollbackKind` are duplicated per family —
    identical shapes, distinct types. Mutation results round-trip through the wire
    form rather than being hand-copied three times; rollback kinds go through a
    macro that names the variants, so a divergence is a compile error.
  - Rollback may write nothing. Its `noOp` arm has no `logEntryVersionId`, which
    is why it has its own result type, and the witness uses exactly that arm.
  - `handshake_timeout_secs` is `NonZeroU64` — the schema's `minimum: 1` — so the
    default is constructed, not unwrapped.

  **Operation futures are boxed, and that is load-bearing.** These handlers fan
  out to four sizeable futures, awaited inside a dispatch match that already
  carries every other task's state machine. Inlining them grew the frame past the
  default 8 MiB stack and aborted an unrelated mock_vta test with a stack
  overflow — which reads as infinite recursion and is not.

- **sdk**: Hold one idempotency key across every attempt of an operation ([#1012](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/pull/1012))

The VTA deduplicates keyed Trust Tasks on an `idempotencyKey` ([#1011](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/pull/1011)).
  That only helps if the retry carries the *same* key as the attempt it is
  retrying — and a hand-rolled retry loop structurally cannot do that,
  because it re-invokes a client method that builds a fresh document each
  time. Minting the key inside the method has the identical problem the
  envelope id already has: attempt two gets a new one, the VTA sees an
  unrelated request, and the second durable effect happens anyway.

  So the key has to be scoped *outside* the call. `VtaClient::idempotent`
  mints one, holds it in a task-local for the duration of a closure, and
  retries transient faults inside that scope:

      let key = client.idempotent(|| client.create_key(req.clone())).await?;

  Every dispatch the closure makes carries the same key. A task-local
  rather than a parameter because it has to reach all twenty-odd typed
  methods without changing twenty signatures, and because it is genuinely
  ambient — it belongs to the operation, not the call.

  The key is attached only when the task is one a second execution would
  actually harm (`retry_safety`); attaching it to a read would cost the
  VTA a dedup record and buy nothing. It goes top-level beside `id`, where
  the VTA reads it from `TrustTask::extra` and a Data-Integrity proof
  covers it — so a relayer cannot rewrite it to split one operation
  into two.

## `vti-common`
## [0.13.0](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/compare/vti-common-v0.12.2...vti-common-v0.13.0) — 2026-08-20 ### Added - **vta**: Dedup keyed Trust Tasks on an idempotency key ([#1011](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/pull/1011)) A client that retries a timed-out request is doing the right thing. ## [0.11.2](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/compare/vta-cli-common-v0.11.1...vta-cli-common-v0.11.2) — 2026-08-20 ### Fixed - **tee**: Bootstrap 410 and vsock enotconn ([#1003](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/pull/1003)) * fix(tee): retry transient ENOTCONN on first vsock config-overlay read tokio-vsock can report a stream connected just before Nitro finishes the nonblocking handshake, so the very first read on a fresh vsock:5800 connection to the parent config server can return ENOTCONN even though the parent is listening and ready. Both omissions changed what an operator ends up with: `tsp` is a default (`default = ["keyring", "tsp"]`) and gates the round-trip TSP probe in `pnm health`. The keyring-free build the README recommended, `--no-default-features --features config-session`, silently dropped it, after which `pnm health` reports an advertised TSPTransport service without ever exercising it. With neither, the backend falls through to the plaintext file store and warns on every access, which is a materially different guarantee from the build-time gate the sentence implied. Replaced with the real selection order, keyring -> azure-secrets -> config-session -> plaintext fallback, and the warning verbatim.

title: ci(semver): a failed baseline means the published crate is broken, so say that
body:
> **Read this first:** `vta-service` does not build on crates.io. That is not
> what I set out to fix — I set out to fix the CI job that reports it, and spent
> most of a day trying to make a true message go away.

## The check was right

`cargo semver-checks` builds its baseline the way a consumer gets it —
`cargo add <crate>@<version>` into a fresh crate, resolved from published ranges
with **no lockfile**. That makes it the only thing in this repo that resolves
like a consumer, and therefore the only thing that can notice when a *published*
artifact stops building.

It noticed. Thirty-second reproduction, nothing of ours in scope:

```
cargo new --lib x && cd x && echo '[workspace]' >> Cargo.toml
cargo add vta-service@0.17.1 && cargo build
→ expected `MediatorAcl`, found a different `MediatorAcl`
→ note: there are multiple different versions of crate `trust_tasks_rs`
```

`affinidi-tdk 0.8.5` → `affinidi-messaging-sdk ^0.19` → resolves to **0.19.9** →
`trust-tasks-rs ^0.11`, while `vta-service` 0.17.1 and `vta-sdk` 0.25.1 require
`^0.9`. The types cross in `vta-sdk`'s `acl_setup`.

**Our builds are fine because `Cargo.lock` pins one of each. Consumers don't get
our lockfile.** That's the whole defect.

| Version | Resolution | Build |
|---|---|---|
| 0.17.1 | split (2) | **fails** — confirmed |
| 0.17.0 | split (2) | not built |
| 0.16.1 | split (3) | **fails** — confirmed |
| 0.15.4 | split (3) | not built |

Blast radius is `vta-service` plus anyone taking `vta-sdk` with the `acl-setup`
feature; default-feature SDK consumers are unaffected.

## Why it hid, which is what this PR changes

Two failures, one expected. The job is `continue-on-error` **by design**, and was
already red for the declared `!` breaks in #1011/#1012 — so a second red looked
like the first. "Baseline failed to build" and "compared, clean" produced the
same silence for that crate.

And the noise **scales with our own output**: every `!` we land raises the floor
and makes the next real finding harder to see. That's a feedback loop, not
ordinary flakiness.

So the step now separates three states that were one:

- **baseline failed to build** → `::error::` naming the crate and the
  reproduction, and saying what it means — not "the check could not run" but
  "consumers cannot build this"
- **compared, breaks reported** → warning (this is what the advisory contract is
  actually about)
- **compared, clean** → says so explicitly

## What this does not do

**It does not gate.** `continue-on-error` is job-level, so `exit 1` is still
soft. The comment says so rather than implying otherwise. Whether "could not
evaluate" should become a real gate is a contract question deserving its own
change — it shouldn't be redefined as a side effect of this.

**It cannot prevent the class.** None of those versions were broken when
published. They broke later, together, when a range they each depend on resolved
somewhere new. No pre-publish check catches a build that breaks two months later,
caused by a release in another repo, on a day nobody touched this one. Only a
check that keeps resolving like a consumer does — which is what this is.

## Rejected alternatives, and why the rejection matters

`--baseline-rev`, `--baseline-root` and `--default-features` were all tried and
all fail identically: the tool always rebuilds the baseline in a fresh isolated
workspace, discarding any lockfile.

That looked like tool inflexibility. **It wasn't.** They were three attempts to
construct a consistent baseline for a crate whose published ranges do not admit
one — and any of them succeeding would have *suppressed a true negative*. The fix
I was reaching for would itself have been the bug.

## Not in this PR — for @stormer78

`vta-service` needs a **release**, and **yank is unavailable**: every published

title: ci(semver): a failed baseline means the published crate is broken, so say that (#1025)
body:
ci(semver): a failed baseline means the published crate is broken, so say that (#1025)

The semver job has been reporting that `vta-service` does not build on
crates.io, and nobody read it that way — including me, for most of a day
spent trying to make the message go away.

## What the check was actually saying

cargo-semver-checks builds its baseline the way a consumer gets it:
`cargo add <crate>@<version>` into a fresh crate, resolved from the
published ranges with no lockfile. That makes it the only thing in this
repo that resolves like a consumer, and so the only thing that can notice
when a published artifact stops building.

It noticed. `vta-service` 0.17.1 does not build for an external consumer:

    cargo new --lib x && cd x && echo '[workspace]' >> Cargo.toml
    cargo add vta-service@0.17.1 && cargo build
    -> expected `MediatorAcl`, found a different `MediatorAcl`
    -> note: there are multiple different versions of crate `trust_tasks_rs`

`affinidi-tdk 0.8.5` requires `affinidi-messaging-sdk ^0.19`, which now
resolves to 0.19.9 requiring `trust-tasks-rs ^0.11`, while 0.17.1 and
`vta-sdk` 0.25.1 require `^0.9`. The types cross in `acl_setup`. Our own
builds are fine because `Cargo.lock` pins one of each; consumers do not
get our lockfile. That is the whole defect.

0.17.0, 0.16.1 and 0.15.4 split the same way — 0.16.1 confirmed by build,
not inferred from the resolution.

## Why it hid

Two failures, one expected. The job is `continue-on-error` by design and
was already red for the `!` breaks in #1011 and #1012, so a second red
looked like the first. "Baseline failed to build" and "compared, clean"
produced the same silence for that crate.

Worse, the noise scales with our own output: every `!` we land raises the
floor and makes the next real finding harder to see.

So the step now separates three states that were one. A baseline that
fails to build gets an `::error::` naming the crate and the reproduction,
and says what it means — not "the check could not run" but "consumers
cannot build this". Reported breaks stay a warning, which is what the
job's advisory contract is actually about.

## What this does not do

It does not gate. The job is `continue-on-error` at job level, so `exit 1`
here is still soft, and the comment says so rather than implying
otherwise. Whether "could not evaluate" should become a real gate is a
contract question that deserves its own change.

It also cannot prevent this class. None of those versions were broken when
published — they broke later, together, when a range they each depend on
resolved somewhere new. No pre-publish check catches a build that breaks
two months later, caused by a release in another repo, on a day nobody
touched this one. Only a check that keeps resolving like a consumer does,
which is what this is.

## Rejected alternatives

`--baseline-rev`, `--baseline-root` and `--default-features` were all
tried and all fail identically; the tool always rebuilds the baseline in a
fresh isolated workspace, discarding any lockfile. That looked like tool
inflexibility. It was not: they were three attempts to construct a
consistent baseline for a crate whose published ranges do not admit one,
and any of them succeeding would have suppressed a true negative.

title: feat(setup): offer to recover a Trust Context that already holds an account
body:
> **Stacked on #249.** Merge #246 → #247 → #248 → #249 first.

## Why

Closes the loop. #247 detects an occupied context; #248 and #249 can plan and build an account from one. This makes that reachable from the wizard, so recovering a lost install is something a user can actually do rather than a capability sitting in the library.

## The flow

`[R]` on the occupied-context page → plan built (read-only) → confirmation page → confirm → `build_state_a_config` writes the rebuilt account with its `key_info`.

```
  Ready to recover this account

    Restores  2 personas, 2 memberships

  This will NOT bring back
    • Community names, favourites and archive flags
    • Relationships and their peer DIDs
    • Contacts and the names you gave them
    • Activity history and pending join requests

  Credentials that did not verify
    • bad-0 — it expired on 2020-01-01T00:00:00Z

  Nothing has been written yet. Press [ENTER] to recover.
```

## Three calls worth reviewing

**The gaps carry the same weight as the wins.** A user who expects contacts and relationships back and finds them missing concludes the recovery *failed* — and may re-run setup, which is the one thing that would make it worse. So `known_gaps()` renders as prominently as the summary of what returns.

**Enter is gated on there being something usable.** A plan whose personas could not have their keys mapped produces an account that cannot sign, so the page says *"Nothing here can be recovered"* and does not offer to proceed. Offering would be a lie, and a confirmation key that silently does nothing is worse than an absent one.

**A failed recovery cannot silently write an empty account.** `build_state_a_config` falls back to the fresh path when the plan failed *or* produced nothing usable. Three tests cover all three paths — this failure mode would be quiet and destructive.

## What still comes from this run, not the old profile

The VTA relationship and the protection choice. The recovering install was authorised separately and holds its own credential; the profile is protected on *this* machine by whatever the operator picks, not by whatever the lost one used.

## Note

The new action is grouped explicitly with its setup-only siblings in both runtime matches — the #236 exhaustiveness work required that rather than letting it fall through a wildcard. Worth knowing if you add actions.

## Known gap

**D5's diff is not implemented.** Recovery currently runs only during setup, where there is nothing to diff against — so the gap is latent rather than live. It becomes real the moment recovery is reachable from Settings, and that should land before it is.

Both feature configurations green, clippy clean.

title: feat(setup): offer to recover a Trust Context that already holds an account (#250)
body:
feat(setup): offer to recover a Trust Context that already holds an account (#250)

* feat(rebuild): turn a verified plan into an account

The write half of recovery: personas, their key_info, and memberships
carrying their own credentials.

The part that decides whether recovery actually works is key_info — the map
from each verification-method id in a DID document to the VTA key backing
it. Without it a rebuilt persona cannot sign, encrypt or connect, and is a
record that fails on first use. At mint time the mapping is free: the DID
creation response hands back signing_key_id and ka_key_id alongside the DID.
A rebuild has neither. It has a list of DIDs and a list of keys and must
re-establish the correspondence.

`vta_sdk::did_secrets::select_secret_kid` is the VTA's own rule for that
question, so it is what gets used rather than a second implementation that
could disagree — the same discipline the project already applies to
didwebvh-rs and agent-names. A key belongs to a persona when the store's
key_id is a verification-method id of that DID, or when its label is.

That rule can fail: a VTA storing keys under opaque ids with free-text
labels leaves the correspondence unrecoverable. Such a persona is EXCLUDED
and reported rather than written into the account, matching what
config::integrity does for a degraded load and for the same reason — a
broken persona in the account is worse than a named absence. A test covers
the mixed case, where one persona maps and another does not.

Memberships are rebuilt Active by construction, because the community
signed a membership credential for that persona and that is what being a
member is. Each record keeps its VMC, so a rebuilt membership carries its
own proof rather than resting on the VTA's word. A membership whose persona
was skipped is dropped — its credential verified fine, but there is nothing
left to attach it to.

`apply` is pure: no network, no disk. The caller decides whether to persist,
which is where D5's diff-and-confirm belongs — silently overwriting local
state from a server view is how a stale VTA destroys good local data.

Two honest gaps, both visible in the code rather than papered over.
Persona `created_at` is stamped `now`, because the VTA records when the DID
was minted, not when OpenVTC first knew of it, and inventing a past date
would be a lie. Sub-context ids are reconstructed by convention; the real
ones return with the rest of the soft state once E2 lands.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.g@affinidi.com>

* docs: drop a redundant explicit link target

rustdoc rejects `[`Name`](path::Name)` when the label already resolves to
the same destination. Caught by the Documentation job, which runs cargo doc
with -D warnings — a different lint set from clippy.

No behaviour change.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.g@affinidi.com>

* feat(setup): offer to recover a Trust Context that already holds an account

Closes the loop. The probe already detected an occupied context and the
rebuild engine could already plan and build an account from one; this makes
that reachable from the wizard, so recovering a lost install is something a
user can actually do rather than a capability sitting in the library.

`[R]` on the occupied-context page builds a plan and shows it. That step is
strictly read-only — `rebuild::plan` lists and verifies, `rebuild_apply` is
pure — so the confirmation page can state plainly that nothing has been
written, which it does in every one of its four states. The write happens on

make it worse. So `known_gaps()` is rendered as prominently as the summary
of what returns. Rejected credentials and skipped personas are listed for

title: feat(bindings): https 0.2 — define what the advertised endpoint denotes
body:
## The gap

§2 has always fixed the request path at `/trust-tasks`. **Nothing said what that
path is relative to**, or how a producer holding only a consumer's DID finds it.

That is not academic. Two readings are defensible against 0.1:

| reading | composes |
|---|---|
| append the path from §2 | `<serviceEndpoint>` + `/trust-tasks` |
| the advertisement *is* the endpoint | POST to `<serviceEndpoint>` directly |

They are not interoperable, and deployments have shipped each. This surfaced
when a client built from this binding and a client built from an SDK composed
the URL differently — and both were conformant, because the spec never said
which was right. Two implementations agreeing by convention is not a contract;
it hides the absence of one from the people best placed to notice.

## What 0.2 adds

**§6.1 — the Trust-Task base.** The advertised value is the *base*; the request
URL is `<serviceEndpoint> + "/trust-tasks"`. A trailing `/` is ignored rather
than producing an empty segment.

**§6.2 — the service entry.** `type: TrustTaskHTTPS`, matched on **type** and
never on the `id` fragment, which is an arbitrary controller-chosen label.

The name states an **interface** — "this party accepts Trust Task documents over
the HTTPS binding" — not a product. That distinction is load-bearing rather than
stylistic: a party's Trust-Task endpoint and its general REST API are *different
claims* that merely coincide in some deployments. A consumer that conflates them
sends Trust Tasks to an endpoint that never agreed to accept them.

**§6.3 — out-of-band configuration stays conformant.** Discovery is not made
mandatory. Where both exist, prefer the advertisement: it is the value the
consumer controls and can rotate, and a stale configured base outlives the
consumer's ability to move.

**§6.4 — ordering.** Capability discovery (§7, renumbered from §6) cannot come
first. A discovery request is *itself* a Trust Task document sent over this
binding, so a producer that cannot compose the URL cannot ask what the consumer
supports.

## Why only this binding needed it

Worth stating in the spec rather than leaving as folklore:

- **DIDComm** resolves `DIDCommMessaging` — owned by the DID Specification Registries
- **TSP** resolves a VID through TSP's own mechanism
- **HTTPS** had no owning specification for its address

HTTPS is the only binding in this family whose address belonged to nobody, which
is precisely why two conforming implementations could disagree about it. The
sibling bindings aren't better specified here by accident — they inherited an
answer from elsewhere.

## Versioning

A new `MINOR` per §8: additive only, no existing requirement changed, `0.1`
retained. Same shape as `didcomm` 0.1 → 0.2 in #186.

## Verification

- `npm run validate` — 337 specs, no errors
- `npm run check-bindings` — 337 specs against 337 TypeScript and 332 Rust modules, all agree

The registry-site entry is included: `npm run validate` **failed** without it
("would be published and unreachable from the registry site"), which is the
check doing its job.

## Note for reviewers

The naming call is the part most worth arguing with. `TrustTaskHTTPS` follows
the principle that service types name protocols rather than products — the same
reasoning that gives a Trust Registry its own REST type instead of borrowing an
agent's. If the task force prefers a different name, the mechanism in §6 stands
unchanged; only the token moves.

title: security(deps): clear four Dependabot alerts by moving the edges that carry them
body:
Four open alerts on the default branch, two high. Neither is a version bump,
and neither means quite what the severity implies — so both are diagnosed to
the edge that carries them rather than bumped and hoped.

## `quinn-proto` 0.11.14 (high) — real pin, no exposure

Remote memory exhaustion from unbounded out-of-order buffering; patched in
0.11.15. It lives in `deploy/nitro/enclave-proxy/Cargo.lock`, which is a
separate lockfile from the workspace — that is how it drifted.

**It is never compiled.** It arrives as an optional dependency of `reqwest`'s
HTTP/3 support, which this crate does not enable:

```
cargo tree -i quinn-proto              -> nothing to print
cargo tree -i quinn-proto --target all -> nothing to print
cargo build --locked                   -> quinn never compiles
```

Cargo records optional dependencies in the lockfile whether or not the
feature selecting them is on, and Dependabot reads the lockfile rather than
the build graph. The alert is accurate about the pin and silent about the
fact that nothing links it.

Bumped anyway. The pin is what the alert is about, and leaving a
known-vulnerable version pinned so that a future feature flip can quietly
link it is worse than a one-line lock change. It also clears a high alert
that would otherwise keep drawing attention away from ones that bite.

## `rustls-webpki` ×3 — a misleadingly-named feature, not a stale version

All three alerts resolve to a single `0.101.7`, **not** to the `0.103.14` the
workspace also carries. Nothing in this tree names `rustls-webpki`, so no
bump can move it. Worth stating plainly, because "two high alerts, one is
just a patch" invites someone to try the bump, watch the alert survive, and
conclude the tooling is wrong.

The copy arrives through a feature edge:

```
aws-sdk-{kms,dynamodb} default features -> "rustls"
  -> aws-smithy-runtime/tls-rustls
  -> aws-smithy-http-client/legacy-rustls-ring
  -> rustls 0.21.8 -> rustls-webpki 0.101.7
```

**The `rustls` feature on those SDK crates does not mean "use rustls".** It
selects the *legacy* ring-backed rustls 0.21 client. The modern stack was
already in the tree — `rustls-aws-lc` on rustls 0.23, reached via
`default-https-client` — so the legacy pull was redundant as well as
vulnerable, and this workspace has been compiling both TLS stacks.

`default-features = false` plus the features actually wanted removes it.
Afterwards neither `rustls@0.21.12` nor `rustls-webpki@0.101.7` is in the
resolved graph on any target; only `0.23.43` / `0.103.14` remain.

### The lockfile does not change

Zero churn, and that is the evidence the legacy client was never needed —
nothing else in the tree was reaching it.

It also means **the alerts may not close**, for the same reason as
`quinn-proto`: the optional-dependency entries persist in the lock, and
Dependabot reads the lock. What changes is that the code is no longer
compiled or linked. Flagging so nobody reads a surviving alert as this change
having failed.

## Verification

The change touches the KMS/DynamoDB path used by the enclave, so it is
verified against the exact CI invocations that reach `vta-tee`:

| run | result |
|---|---|
| `cargo test --workspace` | exit 0, 145 suites, 0 failed |
| `cargo test -p vta-tee --features tenant-overlay tenant_overlay` | exit 0 |
| `cargo test -p vta-service --no-default-features --features tee,rest,didcomm --lib routes::bootstrap` | exit 0 |

## Unrelated, found while verifying — not fixed here

`cargo test --workspace --all-features` does not compile on a clean `main`:
six `E0609`s in `vta-sdk/tests/provision_client_e2e.rs`, reading `.nonce` and
`.holder` off a `serde_json::Value`. Confirmed pre-existing by stashing this
change and reproducing. CI runs `cargo test --workspace` (ci.yml:203) plus
targeted feature combos and never `--all-features`, so nothing covers it.
Reported rather than folded in.

## Checklist (stack guide §9)

- [x] No new `reqwest::Client::new()` / bare `fetch()` (R1.2)
- [x] No lock held across a network await (R1.3)
- [x] No local state committed before its remote effect (R2.1)
- [x] Every retry bounded + backed off (R1.4)
- [x] Accept/poll/listen loops survive transient errors (R1.5)
- [x] Acks/deletes happen only after durable handoff (R1.6)
- [x] New/changed wire types (R3.*) — none
- [x] Config absence = most restrictive (R5.*) — `default-features = false`
      is exactly this: nothing is pulled that is not named
- [x] **Logs/status claim only what was verified (R6.\*)** — states that the
      alerts may survive the fix, rather than implying they close

title: feat(rebuild): turn a verified plan into an account (#249)
body:
feat(rebuild): turn a verified plan into an account (#249)

* feat(rebuild): turn a verified plan into an account

The write half of recovery: personas, their key_info, and memberships
carrying their own credentials.

The part that decides whether recovery actually works is key_info — the map
from each verification-method id in a DID document to the VTA key backing
it. Without it a rebuilt persona cannot sign, encrypt or connect, and is a
record that fails on first use. At mint time the mapping is free: the DID
creation response hands back signing_key_id and ka_key_id alongside the DID.
A rebuild has neither. It has a list of DIDs and a list of keys and must
re-establish the correspondence.

`vta_sdk::did_secrets::select_secret_kid` is the VTA's own rule for that
question, so it is what gets used rather than a second implementation that
could disagree — the same discipline the project already applies to
didwebvh-rs and agent-names. A key belongs to a persona when the store's
key_id is a verification-method id of that DID, or when its label is.

That rule can fail: a VTA storing keys under opaque ids with free-text
labels leaves the correspondence unrecoverable. Such a persona is EXCLUDED
and reported rather than written into the account, matching what
config::integrity does for a degraded load and for the same reason — a
broken persona in the account is worse than a named absence. A test covers
the mixed case, where one persona maps and another does not.

Memberships are rebuilt Active by construction, because the community
signed a membership credential for that persona and that is what being a
member is. Each record keeps its VMC, so a rebuilt membership carries its
own proof rather than resting on the VTA's word. A membership whose persona
was skipped is dropped — its credential verified fine, but there is nothing
left to attach it to.

`apply` is pure: no network, no disk. The caller decides whether to persist,
which is where D5's diff-and-confirm belongs — silently overwriting local
state from a server view is how a stale VTA destroys good local data.

Two honest gaps, both visible in the code rather than papered over.
Persona `created_at` is stamped `now`, because the VTA records when the DID
was minted, not when OpenVTC first knew of it, and inventing a past date
would be a lie. Sub-context ids are reconstructed by convention; the real
ones return with the rest of the soft state once E2 lands.

* docs: drop a redundant explicit link target

rustdoc rejects `[`Name`](path::Name)` when the label already resolves to
the same destination. Caught by the Documentation job, which runs cargo doc
with -D warnings — a different lint set from clippy.

title: feat(rebuild): reconstruct an account from what the VTA holds (D8, D18)
body:
> **Stacked on #247.** Merge #246 → #247 first.

## Why

The read half of recovery: given a Trust Context, work out what an account rebuilt from it would contain, and verify every part of it.

## The finding that changes the sequencing

**Memberships do not need the application-state store (E2) to come back.**

A `MembershipCredential` names its issuer (the community's VTC) and its subject (one of your personas) — which is *exactly* the pair that defines a membership. So a membership is not looked up from the VTA and then checked against a credential; it is **read out of** the credential.

Reconstruction and verification become the same act, which makes D18 nearly free and means rebuild delivers considerably more than the spec's ordering assumed: personas, keys **and** verified memberships, with E2 still outstanding.

## What D18 is actually defending against

Today the local config is the source of truth, so a hostile VTA cannot invent a membership. Rebuilding from the VTA removes that property — unless the membership comes from something the community *signed*, which is what this does. Fabricating a membership would require fabricating a credential.

## Rejections are typed, not collapsed

A credential that fails is neither silently dropped nor silently accepted. It lands in `rejected` with a typed reason, and the user decides — the same shape `config::integrity` uses for a degraded load.

The reasons are kept apart rather than collapsed into one "invalid" string because each is a different decision: a credential for another persona is somebody else's; an expired one may be re-issuable; a malformed validity window is a bug somewhere.

**Validity mirrors the existing VIC rule deliberately:** absent means non-expiring (the community re-checks at use), and **malformed fails closed**, because an unreadable window is not an open one.

## Reads only

`plan` returns what *would* be rebuilt so the caller can show it and ask (D5). Silently overwriting local state from a server view is how a stale VTA destroys good local data.

A credential-vault failure degrades the plan to personas-only rather than failing it — personas and their keys are the larger half of an account.

`known_gaps()` states what will not come back. A recovery screen silent about its gaps leaves the user to conclude the recovery failed when their contacts do not reappear.

## Review notes

14 tests, all pure — the verification logic needs no VTA. The vault envelope handling accepts a bare array and the common wrappers, and unwraps rows carrying the credential under `credential`/`vc`; reporting zero credentials on a full vault would make the plan lie.

body:
feat(rebuild): reconstruct an account from what the VTA holds (D8, D18) (#248)

* feat(setup): stop writing into a Trust Context that is already in use

Setup took a VTA DID and a context id and started creating things without
ever checking what was already there. Pointing a fresh install at a context
you already use silently minted a SECOND set of personas beside the first,
and a mistyped context id was indistinguishable from a deliberate one until
much later — by which point both accounts existed.

The moment setup holds an authenticated client it can simply look. Three
list calls answer it, all three already exist, and no VTA change is needed
(D5, D6). The probe runs during provisioning so the answer is ready when
the operator presses Enter, rather than introducing a pause they would
experience as a hang.

`ProbeOutcome` deliberately separates "empty" from "could not tell".
Conflating them is exactly how a probe turns back into a silent collision,
so an inconclusive listing leaves setup behaving precisely as it always
has — failing to inform the decision must not prevent making it.

The summary counts rather than gestures (D7): "3 personas, 2 sub-contexts
and 14 credentials", not "existing content found". The user is deciding
whether this is THEIR account and needs enough detail to tell, so the page
also lists the first few persona DIDs.

Two deliberate omissions on the page.

Recover is not offered. Rebuilding a context needs the rebuild path and the
application-state store behind it, and an option that cannot complete is
worse than one that is absent — so the page says plainly that recovery is
not available yet and points at the encrypted export, which does work
today. It also states outright that continuing is NOT recovery, because
that is the misreading that would make this screen actively harmful.

Delete is not on the screen at all (D11). Destroying a context takes its
persona DIDs and their keys with it, irreversibly, and that must never be
one keypress from someone who re-ran setup. "Use a different context" is
the non-destructive way to start fresh, and it is the first option offered.

Continuing is bound to [C], not Enter: it means adding a second account
beside the first, and that deserves a deliberate keystroke rather than the
one the operator has been pressing to advance every page so far.

Sub-context matching requires the separator, so `openvtc-2` is not counted
as a child of `openvtc` — otherwise every account on a shared VTA would
look occupied. The credential count tolerates the vault envelope key
moving, since reporting zero credentials on a full vault would make the

title: fix(storage): durable Linux secrets, fail-closed, and diagnosable startup failures
body:
## Why

A user hit `Config Error: Couldn't find openvtc secured configuration. Reason: No matching credential found` and was told to **check their network**. Both halves of that were wrong, and chasing it down turned up a data-loss bug plus three latent ones.

**This branch is independent of the four recovery PRs stacked on it and can merge alone.** It is also the only one fixing something currently hurting users.

## The data loss

`linux-keyutils-keyring-store` documents itself as RAM-only — *"completely in-memory and will not persist across reboots. Consider the keyring a secure cache"* — and OpenVTC registered it unconditionally on Linux as the **sole home** of a profile's BIP32 seed / VTA credential bundle. A reboot, a logout, or three days of the persistent keyring's default expiry destroyed the account.

OpenVTC was the only tool in the workspace doing this. `pnm`, `vta-service`, `vtc-service` and `cnm` all use Secret Service via `vta_sdk::keyring_init::install_default_store`. Store registration now delegates to that same call, so every tool puts secrets in the same place on the same OS.

**And it now fails closed.** If the credential store cannot be opened, OpenVTC exits with an explanation rather than quietly writing keys somewhere weaker. Headless machines opt in deliberately with `OPENVTC_SECURE_STORE=file` — a new encrypted-file store at mode `0600` that *refuses* an unencrypted profile, so key material is never written to disk in the clear.

## The advice

One fixed hint — *"Check your network and that your VTA/mediator are reachable"* — was shown for a missing credential, a locked keychain, a wrong passphrase and a corrupt blob alike. That is what dev-guide **R6.4** exists to forbid.

`OpenVTCError` gained a typed `SecureStore { fault }` variant, and a new `diagnostics` module turns each into its own report: what failed, what it means, the state of the config file and credential store, commands to confirm it, and remedies in order. Restore always precedes the destructive reset, and no reset is offered at all for a locked store or a wrong passphrase — the keys are intact in both.

## Three more, found on the way

- **One half-written persona took down the entire profile.** A crash between `Config::save`'s two writes left a persona with no `key_info`, and key rehydration failed the *whole* load — every other persona, community and relationship. Now the fault is isolated to the persona that has it, the rest loads, and the user acknowledges a report. `Config::save` also now writes secrets **before** the config file, so a crash leaves the persona absent rather than broken.
- **D12** — `ProtectedConfig`'s key was `HKDF(admin_credential_private_key, …)`, making one value both a rotatable authorisation grant and a data-at-rest key that must never change. The profile now carries its own random key.
- **D19** — `Account`/`PersonaRecord`/`CommunityRecord`/`ProtectedConfig` silently dropped fields from newer builds. Each now preserves them.

## Review notes

- `openvtc/src/main.rs` — the fail-closed policy and its message.
- `openvtc-core/src/diagnostics.rs` — tests pin that a local failure never advises checking the network, and that restore precedes reset.
- `decrypt_protected_with_fallback` is extracted specifically so the D12 migration is testable without a TDK/keyring/network — it is the one place a wrong answer locks a user out. **Verified against a real pre-D12 profile.**
- `CommunityRecord`'s D19 catch-all had to go on its *shadow*; on the record it compiles and still drops everything. There is a test for that mistake.

## Also included

`docs/design/vta-authoritative-state.md` — the spec the four stacked PRs implement.

## Known gaps, recorded not fixed

- Unrecognised *credential kinds* are still dropped by `CommunityRecordShadow`; preserving them needs a serialize-side shadow too.
- `SecuredConfig::load` still runs inside an async context — safe with the synchronous dbus client, but a keyring unlock prompt would hold a worker thread.
- A crash during a **passphrase change** still bricks a profile in either write order, because `assert_format_matches_intent` refuses a format/protection mismatch. That is the downgrade defence working as designed; solving it needs a real two-store transaction.

Both feature configurations green, clippy clean at `-D warnings`.
