title: fix(storage): durable Linux secrets, fail-closed, and diagnosable startup failures (#246)
body:
fix(storage): durable Linux secrets, fail-closed, and diagnosable startup failures (#246)

* fix(storage): make Linux secret storage durable, and startup failures diagnosable

A user hit `Config Error: Couldn't find openvtc secured configuration.
Reason: No matching credential found` and was told to check their network.
Both halves of that were wrong.

The store. `linux-keyutils-keyring-store` documents itself as RAM-only —
"completely in-memory and will not persist across reboots. Consider the
keyring a secure cache and plan for your application to handle cases where
the entry is no longer available" — and OpenVTC registered it
unconditionally on Linux as the sole home of a profile's BIP32 seed / VTA
credential bundle. A reboot, a logout, or the persistent keyring's 3-day
default expiry destroyed the account. The README meanwhile described a
Secret Service backend with automatic fallback that the code never had.

Linux now tries Secret Service first (durable, and what the README claimed),
and where none answers falls back to a new encrypted-file store under
`~/.config/openvtc/secrets/` at mode 0600. That store refuses an
unencrypted blob, so an unprotected profile is never silently written to
disk in the clear — it stays in the kernel keyring, and the user is now told
so at startup and in Settings, beside the two actions that fix it. Setting a
passphrase migrates the secret to disk and clears the volatile copy.
`OPENVTC_SECURE_STORE` overrides the choice. `dbus-secret-service-keyring-store`
rather than the zbus variant because affinidi-tdk-common already pulls it in
— one Secret Service client in the graph, and a synchronous one, which suits
our blocking save path.

The advice. The loading screen printed one fixed line — "Check your network
and that your VTA/mediator are reachable" — for every startup failure,
including a missing credential, a locked keychain, a wrong passphrase and a
corrupt blob, pointing the user away from the machine the problem was on.
That is the practice dev-guide R6.4 exists to forbid. `OpenVTCError` gained a
typed `SecureStore { fault, .. }` variant so those cases stay
distinguishable, and a new `diagnostics` module turns each into its own
report: what failed, what it means, the state of the config file and the
credential store, commands to confirm it, and remedies in order. Restore
always precedes the destructive reset, and no reset is offered at all for a
locked store or a wrong passphrase, where the keys are intact. The report
scrolls, and is written to `last-startup-failure.txt` for bug reports.

`openvtc health` now leads with that local picture and runs when no account
can be loaded at all — previously it aborted with "nothing to check", which
is precisely the run where the answer was wanted.

Verified end to end: a profile with a config file and no credential now
reports `credential NOT FOUND`, names the store and the exact `security`
command to confirm it, and exits 1.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.g@affinidi.com>

* fix(load): isolate a broken persona instead of failing the whole profile

A profile is saved in two writes, not one: the config file (carrying the
account, and with it the persona records) and then the SecuredConfig blob
in the OS credential store (carrying key_info). They are not atomic, so a
crash part-way through creating a persona left the account recording a
persona whose keys were never written.

That was fatal for everything. `regenerate_persona_keys` returned Err on
the first verification method with no key_info, the error propagated out of
the persona loop, and the entire load failed — every other persona, every
community, every relationship — with a message naming a verification method
id, which tells the user nothing about what happened or what to do.

Now the fault is isolated to the persona that has it. Each persona hydrates
independently and a failure is recorded rather than thrown: everything
loadable loads, and what could not is gathered into a LoadIntegrity report.
`regenerate_persona_keys` returns a typed DegradedReason because the two
ways it fails need different words in front of the user — an interrupted
write is loss, an unreachable VTA is not, and a formatted string could not
tell them apart.

The startup screen shows that report and turns its continue prompt into an
explicit acknowledgement, so a partially-loaded profile cannot slide
silently into a session where a persona the user believes they have is
quietly absent. It says what is missing, what still works, and what it
means — and states plainly that nothing has been deleted, because that is
true and load-bearing: a degraded persona keeps its record and is skipped,
never dropped. Deleting it would turn a recoverable inconsistency into
permanent loss on the one code path taken by an already-damaged profile.
The report also stays in the activity log, with the acknowledgement
recorded, so it is not ambiguous later whether the user was ever told.

Two supporting changes. A membership whose persona did not load is reported
and can no longer be chosen as the working context — that would put the UI
in a context that cannot send, receive, or sign. And `Config::save` now
writes the secrets BEFORE the config file: both orders lose the persona
that was mid-creation, but file-first leaves an account referencing keys
that do not exist, while secrets-first leaves the persona simply absent and
its leftover keys reported as orphaned key records.

Also fixes the `--no-default-features` build, which CI runs: `use
std::sync::Arc` in state.rs sat behind the openpgp-card feature gate while
`startup_diagnosis` used it unconditionally.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.g@affinidi.com>

* docs(design): spec VTA-authoritative state and reinstall recovery

Proposes moving the account model, memberships, relationships and VRCs to
the VTA so that losing a machine costs a reinstall rather than an account,
and specifies the contract with verifiable-trust-infrastructure for the two
pieces that repo owns.

The finding that shapes the whole spec: half of this is already true.
Persona private keys are escrowed at the VTA and re-fetched on every
startup (KeySourceMaterial::VtaManaged), persona DIDs and documents are
already VTA-authoritative with the local copy a perf cache, and VICs
already live in the credential vault. The rows still local are a migration,
not a new architecture — and because the VTA already holds keys that can
sign as you, storing your membership list there moves no trust boundary
(D1).

What does NOT follow is recovery. The admin credential bundle cannot be
recovered from the VTA because it is what authenticates you to the VTA.
That circularity needs an enrolment step, and the design for it already
exists in the VTI repo as sealed-bootstrap Mode A, with the HPKE primitive
already shipped in vta-sdk::sealed_transfer (E1).

Storage picks agent memory (`vta/memory/{put,list,delete}/0.1`) over the
secrets vault, which is shaped as a password manager, with one key per
record rather than one blob — payload size first, because this project has
already lost a join to a bridge file-size limit silently dropping an
oversized submit. E2 asks VTI for an expectedVersion precondition, since
memory/put is currently last-write-wins.

Nothing settled; D1-D9, E1-E2 and R1-R6 are for review.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.g@affinidi.com>

* docs(design): v2 — the admin credential is an ACL entry, not an identity

Reframes the spec around the point that recovery is re-authorisation, not
key recovery, and corrects two things draft 1 got wrong.

The admin credential is a did:key holding an ACL entry against a context.
The VTA owns that ACL; the credential rotates (spec/acl/swap-key/0.1) and
can be re-issued against an existing context whose content is untouched.
Losing it is losing an authorisation, the same shape as losing an SSH key
listed in authorized_keys. Identity is the persona did:webvh set, and those
already live at the VTA with their private keys.

Correction 1: sealed bootstrap is NOT unimplemented. pnm-cli implements
the whole Mode A flow today — `pnm bootstrap request` produces the
ephemeral recipient key, `pnm context reprovision --id <ctx> --recipient`
mints an admin key for the EXISTING context and seals to it, and `pnm
bootstrap open --expect-digest` consumes it single-use. The
sealed-bootstrap.md status header is stale. E1 shrinks to a self-service
ask: let a passkey- or registered-device-authenticated caller reprovision
without a human in the loop, using primitives the VTA already has.

Correction 2: recovery is a branch in setup, not a command. Setup already
asks for the context id and already authenticates, so the moment it holds
a VtaClient it can probe the context and offer the choice. And "start
fresh" now means use a DIFFERENT context, not destroy this one — deleting
a context destroys persona DIDs and their keys, which must never be one
keypress away from someone who re-ran setup.

New blocker, D12. ProtectedConfig's encryption key is
HKDF(admin_credential_private_key, ...), which makes the credential
simultaneously a rotatable authorisation grant and a data-at-rest key that
must never change. Rotating via acl/swap-key would make the local blob
undecryptable, and a recovered install holds a different admin key, so
recovery and existing local state are mutually exclusive. Not a live bug
(OpenVTC only rotates at provision time, before any ProtectedConfig
exists) but it blocks everything else here. Fix: give ProtectedConfig its
own random key in SecuredConfig, with the same fallback-and-re-encrypt
migration shape as the existing legacy-seed path.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.g@affinidi.com>

* fix(storage): fail closed, and use the same store every other tool uses

Two policy changes to how OpenVTC treats secrets, replacing the automatic
degradation the previous commit still had.

**Never choose a weaker store.** The Linux path used to try Secret Service
and, when none answered, quietly fall back to a composite of the encrypted
file store over the kernel keyring. That is the same practice that makes
vta-sdk's FileBackend write an admin key to plaintext JSON when the keyring
feature is off: the tool decides, the user finds out later. A tool that
silently downgrades its own storage teaches users the secure backend is
optional, and the moment it matters they discover their secrets were
somewhere they never agreed to.

Now, if the OS credential store cannot be opened, OpenVTC exits — with a
message that names the cause and gives the two ways out (start a keyring
daemon, or opt in to file storage). Choosing file storage on a headless
machine is a deliberate act: OPENVTC_SECURE_STORE=file. The composite store
is deleted; it existed only to auto-degrade.

**One implementation across the workspace.** Store registration now
delegates to `vta_sdk::keyring_init::install_default_store` — the same call
pnm-cli makes — so openvtc, pnm and anything else on the SDK put secrets in
the same place on the same OS. OpenVTC was the only tool in the workspace
registering the kernel keyring, and that divergence is the whole bug.

Every store OpenVTC will select is now durable, pinned by a test rather
than left as a comment. `keyutils` remains selectable but is deprecated,
warns loudly on every launch, and is documented as existing only so a
profile written by an older build can be started once and exported.

Unknown OPENVTC_SECURE_STORE values are an error rather than a silent
fall-through to the default, since a typo would otherwise put a profile's
keys somewhere the user did not intend.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.g@affinidi.com>

* docs(design): v3 — concurrency, and E2 becomes a blocker

Adds §9 on what happens when two OpenVTC instances share one Trust Context,
which turns out to be a present-tense bug rather than a future risk.

The messaging layer already breaks on it. The mediator's ceiling is one
websocket per DID and it enforces that by EVICTING the incumbent, so two
instances presenting the same persona each connect, each evicts the other,
and both reconnect-loop. That is the listener-flapping class already
debugged here (openvtc #231, plus the upstream force_refresh fix). Anyone
who opens OpenVTC twice hits it today with none of this spec implemented.
E3 asks the mediator to refuse rather than evict — with displacement kept
as an explicit opt-in, because displacing a socket is also how stored-mail
redelivery is triggered (#218) and a blanket change would regress it.

E2 is promoted from a minor ask to blocking. MemoryItem is {key, value} —
no version, no timestamp, no ETag — so there is nothing to build a
precondition on, and two instances writing one record overwrite each other
with no way to notice afterwards. Per-record keys bound WHICH records
collide; they do nothing about whether a collision is seen. The account
model must not move to agent memory until a precondition exists, or the
migration swaps a local single-writer store for a shared one that corrupts
silently. R2 is rewritten accordingly — "mitigated by per-record keys" was
too generous.

The recommendation is deliberately not a lock. D13 detects siblings using
device registration and heartbeats already in the SDK (DeviceBinding
carries last_seen_at) and needs no VTA change. D14 makes optimistic
concurrency the thing that prevents corruption. D15 adds an advisory,
expiring writer lease only if exclusion is actually wanted, and D15a states
the rule that keeps it honest: the lease reduces conflict, the precondition
prevents corruption — never rely on the lease alone. D16 hands persona
listener ownership to the lease holder so the eviction loop becomes one
working instance and one that explains itself.

Also records two local-lock gaps found while checking: process_lock keys on
the config dir, so two OPENVTC_CONFIG_PATHs with the same profile name both
run, and nothing at all detects two profiles sharing one persona DID.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.g@affinidi.com>

* docs(design): v4 — recovery safety, and withdraw D2a

Adds §10 with the five decisions agreed in review, and corrects one the
earlier drafts got wrong.

D17 — recovery must offer to revoke what it replaced. Recovering mints a
NEW admin ACL entry and leaves the old one valid, so a stolen laptop keeps
a working credential. `delete_acl` / `device_disable` / `device_wipe` all
exist. The prompt defaults to revoking nothing and names each binding by
last-seen, because revoking by default would break the legitimate
two-machine user (D17a), and it stays reachable from Settings afterwards
(D17b).

D18 — verify the rebuilt account model rather than trusting it. Once the
VTA is authoritative it can invent a membership, which today it cannot.
CommunityRecord already carries its VMC, so rebuild verifies each
membership against its own credential and reports failures through the
LoadIntegrity path rather than silently dropping or silently trusting.
This is also why the credential vault and agent memory stay separate
stores (D18b): metadata is only safe in a rewritable store because the
signed artifact backing it lives elsewhere.

D19 — records must survive a round trip through an older build. None of
Account / PersonaRecord / CommunityRecord / ProtectedConfig has
deny_unknown_fields or a catch-all, so unknown fields are silently dropped
on deserialize. Harmless with one writer; data loss the moment two builds
share a store. Fixed with `#[serde(flatten)] extra`, and it must land
before anything writes to agent memory.

D20 — recovery is audited AND provable. Those are different: AuditLogEntry
has no signature and no hash chain, so the VTA's log corroborates but does
not prove. The sealed bundle's ProducerAssertion (DidSigned, or an
attestation quote) is the actual proof, so OpenVTC keeps it as a recovery
receipt (D20a). E4 asks VTI for tamper-evident audit so the log itself can
be evidence.

D21 — recovering a lost VTA is explicitly out of scope. This protects a
lost OpenVTC instance; the encrypted export remains the answer to a lost
agent, and the docs must keep saying so.

D2a is WITHDRAWN. It excluded contacts and the agent-name cache as having
"no recovery value", which was wrong about contacts — a Contact is
{did, alias} and the alias exists nowhere else — and contradicted D2,
which already uploads the relationship graph. A relationship is strictly
more revealing than a contact. D22 syncs both, with every restored cache
entry marked stale on import so the "never display an unverified name"
rule keeps holding: a restored cache is a list of DIDs worth resolving,
not a list of answers. R3 widens accordingly.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.g@affinidi.com>

* docs(design): v5 — rework the external asks

E2 becomes a store design rather than a field. Review asked whether agent
memory is the right home for application metadata at all; it is not.
`vta/memory` is documented as "a per-context key/value store for AI-agent
memory", and clearing an agent's memory is a reasonable user action that
must not take your community memberships with it. That alone settles it —
and `list` has no prefix or pagination either, so an agent's recall and an
application's config would make each other expensive as both grow.

Proposed instead: `spec/vta/appstate/{get,put,list,delete}/1.0`, addressed
by (contextId, namespace, key) so several tools share a context without
colliding. Versions assigned server-side; `expectedVersion` preconditions
whose conflict response CARRIES the current version and value (saving a
round trip and removing the re-read race); `expectedVersion: 0` for
create-only, which is what makes lease acquisition safe; prefix and
pagination on list; `sinceVersion` so write-behind reconcile is
incremental; and tombstones, without which incremental sync cannot
converge because a peer never learns a record was deleted. Value stays
opaque (E2a) and agent memory is untouched (E2b). Three stores, three
jobs: secrets, credentials, application state.

E3 sharpened to "protect the incumbent". Preferring the newcomer means any
second process can silently take over a live authenticated session, and
when both retry they take turns forever. The established connection is
kept and the newcomer refused with a renderable reason. The v4 hedge about
displacement being needed for stored-mail redelivery turns out to be
unnecessary: OpenVTC already collects stored mail explicitly through the
standard message-pickup protocol, so redelivery does not depend on
eviction. E3a keeps confirming that across other clients as a
precondition rather than an assumption, and R9 changes accordingly.

E1 deferred with an explanation of what it actually buys — recovering your
laptop from your already-enrolled phone, with no operator in the loop. It
is convenience, not capability, since the operator path already delivers
recovery.

E4 reframed from tamper-evidence to a pluggable audit sink: a trait the
VTA writes through, with today's database sink as one implementation, so
an append-only log or a blockchain anchor can be a deployment choice
rather than a protocol commitment. D20a already gives the signed,
verifiable recovery receipt where it matters.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.g@affinidi.com>

* docs(design): v6 — batch/blob layers on E2, and E1 becomes DTTE

Two refinements from review, both of which simplify rather than add.

E2 gains three layers, kept distinct so batching and blobs do not undo
D8a. The RECORD stays the unit of correctness — small, individually
versioned, the thing a conflict is reported against. BATCHING is a unit of
transport: get_many/put_many with per-record expectedVersion and
per-record results, so a rebuild or a write-behind flush is one round trip
instead of N. BLOBS are a different class of data: attached to a key,
versioned with their record, never returned by list — only a blobRef with
size and digest.

put_many takes an explicit mode because the two callers want opposite
things. `independent` is the default: one conflicted record must not block
the other nine, which is exactly the blast-radius property D8a exists for.
`atomic` is available for records carrying a joint invariant — minting a
persona and the membership referencing it should not half-land, being the
same two-writes-one-truth problem that produced LoadIntegrity locally. An
atomic default would mean one stale record silently wedging a whole flush.

Blobs reuse the descriptor pattern already in this codebase
(backup_export_via_descriptor → download_blob/upload_blob against a
transport_url, with a wire-level digest check), which keeps large payloads
outside the trust-task envelope and away from the message-size limit that
has already silently dropped a write here. Caveat recorded: that path is
documented REST-only, and OpenVTC speaks DIDComm.

E2f makes values JSON by contract while the store stays schema-agnostic,
which buys merge-patch (RFC 7386) — less payload, and more usefully fewer
CONFLICTS, since two instances editing different fields of one record stop
colliding. E2a is refined accordingly: the store understands JSON, not
your schema.

E1 was wrong in shape and is now DTTE. Delegated Trust-Task Execution
already does this: approvals are a rule list keyed on Trust Task type URI,
`requires: consent` runs the task-consent ceremony, and provisioning is
already dispatched as TASK_PROVISION_INTEGRATION_0_2. So E1 collapses from
new authentication machinery to registering that URI as consent-requiring
with a recovery approver set. Three properties make it the better fit:
approver-set membership alone authorizes (no ACL entry needed, VTI #907),
consent binds to the payload digest rather than elevating a session, and
the approver only ever sees a challenge-salted wire_digest. It also
improves D20 — the decision task is DI-signed by the approver, so an
approved recovery yields a second verifiable artifact proving a human
approved and which one.

D23 adds the product half: nominate a recovery approver BEFORE you need
one. An approver set established at recovery time is not a recovery
mechanism, it is a formality.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.g@affinidi.com>

* fix(config): give the profile its own encryption key, and stop dropping fields

The two blockers from the VTA-authoritative-state spec (D12, D19). Both are
prerequisites: nothing that shares config records with another install is
safe to build until they are in.

D12 — decouple the ProtectedConfig key from the admin credential.

The key was HKDF(admin_credential_private_key, "openvtc-protected-config-
seed-v1"), which made one value serve two irreconcilable roles: an
authorisation grant designed to rotate (acl/swap-key) and be re-issued to a
recovering install, and a data-at-rest key that must never change. Rotating
would have made the on-disk config undecryptable, and a recovered install
necessarily holds a different credential, so recovery and existing local
state could never coexist.

SecuredConfig now carries `protected_key`: 32 random bytes from the OS
CSPRNG, base64url, living beside the credential bundle under the same
passphrase or token. `Config::get_encryption_seed` prefers it and falls
back to the old derivation only for a config that predates it.

The load-side decision is extracted as `decrypt_protected_with_fallback`
precisely because it is the one place a wrong answer locks a user out of
their own profile — it needs to be testable without a TDK, a keyring or a
network. It tries three keys newest-first: the stored key, the pre-D12
derivation, and the pre-0.1.4 BIP32 verifying-key seed. Anything but the
first sets a re-key flag completed on the next save.

Keeping the older keys readable is not politeness, it is R7: Config::save
writes the secured blob BEFORE the public one, so a crash between the two
leaves the new key stored and the old blob still on disk. A test pins that
an interrupted re-key still opens the profile.

Verified against a real pre-D12 profile: it loads, and logs "config
predates its own encryption key; re-keying on next save".

D19 — preserve fields written by newer builds.

Account, PersonaRecord, CommunityRecord and ProtectedConfig had neither
deny_unknown_fields nor a catch-all, so serde silently discarded anything
unrecognised. One writer meant it never mattered; two writers at different
versions makes it data loss by round trip. Each gains a
`#[serde(flatten)] extra`, skipped when empty so existing configs stay
byte-identical.

CommunityRecord's catch-all had to go on CommunityRecordShadow, not the
record: the shadow deserializes first, so a flatten on the record compiles
and still drops everything. There is a test for exactly that mistake.

Known gap, recorded rather than half-fixed: CommunityRecordShadow also
drops unrecognised *credential kinds* with a warning. Preserving those
needs a serialize-side shadow too, or the round trip re-emits them in the
wrong place and a newer build cannot find its own credential.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.g@affinidi.com>

* feat(devices): show when another install is using this account (D13)

OpenVTC's only concurrency guard is a PID lock file keyed on the config
directory and profile name. It catches one case — the same profile started
twice from the same config path — and misses two config paths, two profile
names sharing a persona, and two machines entirely.

That gap is not theoretical. The mediator's ceiling is one websocket per
DID and it enforces it by EVICTING the established connection, so two
installs presenting the same persona take turns evicting each other and
both reconnect-loop. It presents as a network fault rather than as "you
have this open twice" — the listener-flapping class already debugged here.

This does not fix that (E3 asks the mediator to protect the incumbent). It
makes it visible, which needs no VTA change: a DeviceBinding is the
device-facing half of an AclEntry, each install already has its own, and
the binding carries lastSeenAt. Register on connect, heartbeat every five
minutes, list on each beat, and say who else is here.

Everything is best-effort. Registration is diagnostic, not functional, so
a VTA without the device slice or one briefly unreachable costs a log line
and nothing else. The task is spawned rather than awaited, so it cannot
delay startup by a frame, and it never touches State — reports go down a
channel the loop owns, preserving the single-mutator rule.

Two judgement calls worth naming. Liveness is three heartbeat intervals,
not one: a false "nobody else is here" is the worse error, because it is
the one that walks a user into the eviction loop believing they are alone.
And a device whose clock runs ahead of ours is treated as live, because
skew is not staleness.

The announce set is keyed on device id, not the whole record: lastSeenAt
changes every beat, so comparing records would re-warn about the same
machine every five minutes, and a warning shown that often is one people
learn to scroll past. A sibling that goes away is forgotten, so closing
and reopening announces it again — that is a fresh collision.

The consumerKind is companion/desktop, and the camelCase wire form was
checked against the VTA's own kind_to_wire rather than the internal type,
which is kebab-cased and never crosses the wire (dev-guide R3.6).

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.g@affinidi.com>

* docs: fix intra-doc links that failed the Documentation job

CI runs `cargo doc --workspace --no-deps` with `RUSTDOCFLAGS=-D warnings`,
which is a different lint set from clippy — broken and ambiguous intra-doc
links are caught there and nowhere else. All three failures are in
module-level or item docs added by this branch:

- `[`Config::save`]` in config/integrity.rs. Module-level `//!` docs resolve
  in *that file's* scope, and `Config` is not in scope there, so the link
  needs the full path. Same family as the trap already documented in
  openvtc-core/src/lib.rs about outer docs on `pub mod`.
- `[`ProtectedConfig`]` in secured_config.rs — same cause, on an item doc.
- `[`file`]` in secure_store/mod.rs is ambiguous: `file` is both the module
  being referenced and a macro in scope. Disambiguated with `mod@`.

No behaviour change.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.g@affinidi.com>

---------

title: feat(service): retire an orphaned webvh slot, on evidence rather than assertion
body:
Closes the last item on #1009. Implements `vta/webvh/servers/retire-orphan/0.1`
(spec: trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf#249).

## The gap

`vta/webvh/servers/reconcile` reports two divergences and repairs neither,
deliberately, because they want opposite remedies. The `agentOnly` side has one —
retry the publish, or drop the local record. The `hostOnly` side, an **orphan**,
had none, and the reason is structural rather than an oversight:

Every delete addresses a DID *through its local record* — that record is what says
which server to talk to and which keys to sign with. An orphan is defined by that
record's absence, so `get_did(...).ok_or(NotFound)` fails before a request ever
leaves the VTA. And the caller can't go around it: reconcile authenticates to the
host with VTA-held credentials, so the VTA *is* the credential holder.

A slot both parties can see, and neither can remove.

## The one property everything rests on

**The VTA decides whether the slot is orphaned. The caller does not get to claim
it.**

A slot id is a bare string. If this trusted it, the operation would be "delete
anything on the host, unaudited by the VTA's own state" wearing a narrower name.
Instead it re-runs the same comparison `reconcile` performs and refuses if it
holds *any* record for the slot — a live DID has a record, and that record is what
makes the refusal automatic.

If you review one thing, review whether `decide_retirement` actually closes that.

I lifted it out of the I/O, the way `diff_host_against_local` already is in the
same file, so every refusal is testable without a host. Three of the nine tests
exist only because of that: a record naming a **different** server doesn't shield
the slot, and `expectedDid` fires in both directions — expected-a-DID-got-none as
well as got-a-different-one.

## Refusing under uncertainty is deliberate

Three conditions decline. Two are *uncertainty* rather than contradiction — the
listing is unobtainable, or the DID doesn't match — meaning the VTA doesn't know
the slot is safe to remove. The asymmetry settles it: the alternative to a false
refusal is a retry; the alternative to a false removal is nothing.

## Classification

- **`Destructive`** in the dispatch table, not `Mutating`. It stops a published
  identifier resolving, and every relying party that held the DID sees that
  without being able to distinguish retirement from compromise or an outage.
- **`RetrySafe`** in `retry_safety`. Destructive but convergent — once the slot is
  gone a repeat removes nothing. The slot-reuse hazard is closed twice: the
  orphanhood re-derivation, and `expectedDid`.
- **Never automatic.** Nothing calls it on a timer and nothing should. The signal
  is an *absence*, and absences come from bugs as readily as from orphaning — a
  read that fails open, a record written under the wrong server id. Each presents
  as an orphan, and the response would be to make a published identifier stop
  resolving, irreversibly. The spec forbids it; this just doesn't provide one.

## Two judgement calls to check

**No new error-code machinery.** No extended codes exist anywhere in the
dispatcher today, so the spec's (`retire-orphan:notOrphaned` / `:didMismatch` /
`:listingUnavailable`) ride in `details.reason` — the shape the consent gate uses
and `trust_task_error` already keys on. Making them typed first requires deciding
whether a spec's `errorCodes` are *normative* (should the dispatcher refuse to
emit an undeclared code?), which is a contract question that shouldn't be settled
as a side effect of one family landing. Being raised separately.

**The conformance witness is built from the typed bodies**, not raw JSON — sound
here only because the spec preceded the types. Where a type came first and was
reverse-engineered from a schema, a typed witness can encode the defect and pass
green. See #1021, which writes that rule down.

## Seam

One arm in `trust_tasks/mod.rs`, directly after `SERVERS_RECONCILE`. Coordinated
with the session holding `vta/services/*` — no overlap in `mod.rs`,
`conformance.rs`, or `retry_safety.rs`, and no `api/trust-tasks` references, so
this absorbs #1020's endpoint move cleanly whichever lands first.

## Pre-merge

- [x] `cargo fmt --all --check` — clean
- [x] `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets` — clean
- [x] `cargo test --workspace --no-fail-fast` — 3534 passed, 0 failed
- [x] 9 new unit tests covering every refusal path
- [x] Conformance witness, census, and manifest guards green
- [x] No `version =` edits, no changelog file

title: fix(sdk/service): serve and use the Trust-Task path the binding asks for
body:
## The bug

`trust-tasks-https` — our own published HTTPS binding — POSTs to
`<serviceEndpoint>/trust-tasks`. Every deployment example advertises an
**origin**:

```
docs/02-vta/examples/vta-setup.example.toml   public_url = "https://trust.example.com"
local-dev/vta-pathful-webvh-setup.toml        public_url = "http://localhost:3000"
deploy/nitro/config.toml                    # public_url = "https://vta.example.com"
```

So a client built from the binding asked for `/trust-tasks` and **got a 404**.
Ours worked only because `vta-sdk` hardcoded `/api/trust-tasks` and this service
happened to serve the same prefix.

Two implementations agreeing by convention isn't a contract. It hides the
absence of one from the only people positioned to notice — which is why this
survived until someone read the binding instead of the code.

## The underlying defect was never the path

Nothing defined what the advertised endpoint **denotes**, so the two clients
composed it differently and both could not be right:

| client | composes |
|---|---|
| `vta-sdk` | `<serviceEndpoint>` + `/api/trust-tasks` |
| `trust-tasks-https` | `<serviceEndpoint>` + `/trust-tasks` |

Against an origin advertisement the SDK works and the binding 404s. Against a
`.../api` advertisement the binding works and the SDK **doubles the prefix**.

Settled: **`serviceEndpoint` is the Trust-Task base**, and the binding's suffix
is the contract.

## Why this doesn't break anyone

**The service serves both paths from one dispatcher.** That's the move that
makes it safe: for an origin-advertising VTA the Trust-Task base *is* the
origin, so **every existing advertisement becomes conformant with no operator
action**.

The SDK then moves to `<base>/trust-tasks` — the half that makes the contract
real rather than aspirational — and is safe against any VTA that has taken the
service change.

`/api/trust-tasks` is marked superseded, so the metric governing every other
retired route decides when it goes. It can't go while deployed clients ask for
it, and those clients are our own SDK until this ships.

## One oddity in the superseded table

That row's successor is a **path**, not a task URI. Every other row names the
task that replaced an operation; this one names the endpoint that replaced a
spelling. `Link: rel="successor-version"` takes a URI either way, so the header
stays meaningful — flagged in the comment rather than left looking like an
oversight.

## A second hand-built call site

Moving the SDK surfaced `client/backup_descriptors.rs` formatting
`{base}/api/trust-tasks` itself instead of going through `rpc_tt` — which is
precisely why it kept the legacy prefix after the shared path moved. Same class
as the `update_context` literal in #1015: a payload or URL built by hand drifts
from the one built centrally.

## Tests

Both spellings must reach the same dispatcher **and fail identically when
unauthenticated** — a divergence there means a conformant client and ours behave
differently, which is the thing being fixed. 26 mocks across `client_rest` and
`auth_light_rest` move with the client.

## Not in this PR, on purpose

Specifying what the Trust-Task service entry *means*, so this is a contract
rather than a second convention. That's a spec-registry change and wants its own
review — including whether it deserves a dedicated service `type` rather than
reusing `VTARest`, since "the REST API" and "where Trust Tasks are accepted" are
different claims that merely coincide today.

## Checklist (stack guide §9)

- [x] No new `reqwest::Client::new()` / bare `fetch()` (R1.2)
- [x] No lock held across a network await (R1.3)
- [x] No local state committed before its remote effect (R2.1)
- [x] Every retry bounded + backed off (R1.4)
- [x] Accept/poll/listen loops survive transient errors (R1.5)
- [x] Acks/deletes happen only after durable handoff (R1.6)
- [x] **New/changed wire types (R3.\*)** — no type changed; the endpoint's
      *meaning* is what moved, and the legacy spelling keeps working
- [x] Config absence = most restrictive (R5.*)
- [x] **Logs/status claim only what was verified (R6.\*)** — the superseded row
      says its successor is a path, rather than dressing it as a task
- [x] Deviations flagged with rule numbers

title: fix(sdk,service): serve and use the Trust-Task path the binding asks for (#1020)
body:
fix(sdk,service): serve and use the Trust-Task path the binding asks for (#1020)

`trust-tasks-https` POSTs to `<serviceEndpoint>/trust-tasks`, where
`serviceEndpoint` is what a VTA advertises on its service entry. Every
deployment example advertises an ORIGIN — `https://trust.example.com`,
`http://localhost:3000` — so a client built from the published binding asked
for `/trust-tasks` and got a 404. Ours worked only because `vta-sdk` hardcoded
`/api/trust-tasks` and this service happened to serve the same prefix.

Two implementations agreeing by convention is not a contract; it hides the
absence of one from the only people who would notice — which is why this
survived until someone read the binding rather than the code.

The underlying defect was never the path. Nothing defined what the advertised
endpoint DENOTES, so the two clients composed it differently and both could not
be right: the SDK appended `/api/trust-tasks`, the binding appended
`/trust-tasks`. Settled, per Glenn: **serviceEndpoint is the Trust-Task base**,
and the binding's suffix is the contract.

- **The service serves both.** `/trust-tasks` alongside `/api/trust-tasks`, one
  dispatcher. This is what makes the change safe: for an origin-advertising VTA
  the Trust-Task base IS the origin, so every existing advertisement becomes
  conformant with no operator touching anything.
- **The SDK moved to `<base>/trust-tasks`.** That is the half that makes the
  contract real rather than aspirational, and it is safe against any VTA that
  has taken the change above.
- **`/api/trust-tasks` is marked superseded**, so the metric that governs every
  other retired route decides when it goes. Its successor is a PATH, not a task
  URI — the one row in that table where the successor is not a
  `trusttasks.org` URI, because what replaced it is a spelling rather than an
  operation.

Moving the SDK surfaced a second hand-built call site: `backup_descriptors.rs`
formatted `{base}/api/trust-tasks` itself instead of going through `rpc_tt`,
which is exactly why it kept the legacy prefix after the shared path moved.

Tests pin that both spellings reach the same dispatcher AND fail identically
when unauthenticated — a divergence there would mean a conformant client and
ours behave differently, which is the thing being fixed. 26 mocks across
client_rest and auth_light_rest move with the client.

Still to do, and deliberately not here: specifying what the Trust-Task service
entry means, so this is a contract rather than a second convention. That is a
spec-registry change.

title: docs(service): record why a witness is typed or raw, and when that flips
body:
## Why

The conformance sweep's witnesses are typed for some families and raw JSON for
others, and nothing in the module said why. The reasoning lived only in #1015's
PR body — which is not where someone reading the table will look, and not
somewhere the next person adding a witness will find it.

## The rule

> **Typed when the spec preceded the type, raw JSON when it did not — and the
> second case is a debt.**

A typed witness is the stronger form: it proves *our types* conform, rather than
that someone can hand-write a body the schema accepts.

But it only proves that when the type did not derive its shape from the same
misreading that produced the body. If it did, the witness asserts the code
agrees with itself and passes green straight over the defect.

Not hypothetical — it was the situation when the `vta/contexts/*` and
`vta/webvh/*` schemas arrived (#1015):

| producer type | was sending |
|---|---|
| `create_did_webvh` | `context_id`, against a schema naming `contextId` |
| `update_context` | nothing at all for `contextPolicy` |

Witnesses built from those two would have encoded both defects and reported
conformance. So the 22 went in as raw JSON, with the schema as the authority.

Same principle `scripts/check-bindings-conformance.mjs` applies one layer down
in `dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf`, where the binding rules are deliberately
re-implemented rather than imported from the generator. Its header already makes
the trade explicit: a re-implementation can be wrong, but a wrong one
**disagrees loudly**, where a shared one **agrees silently**.

## What this changes about the pending retro-fit

It makes it legible as a real step rather than tidying. Converting those 22 to
typed bodies is what turns *"the schema accepts a shape someone wrote"* into
*"our types conform"* — and it is sound **only now that #1015 has corrected the
types**. Done before that, it would have laundered the bugs into a green row.

Credit where due: this framing came out of a working exchange with the session
on the retirement branch, who had been carrying it as the weaker "typed is
better, retro-fit later" and asked that the sharper version be written down
rather than left in a conversation.

## Scope

Module docs only. No behaviour change, no witness moved, no type touched.
`cargo check -p vta-service --all-features` clean, zero warnings.

title: fix(tee): bootstrap 410 and vsock enotconn
body:
tokio-vsock can report a stream connected just before Nitro finishes the
nonblocking handshake, so the very first read on a fresh vsock:5800
connection to the parent config server can return ENOTCONN even though
the parent is listening and ready. Retry only that specific transient
error kind with a short delay; any other I/O error still fails closed
immediately, and the existing overall READ_TIMEOUT deadline still
bounds the whole fetch.

Adds positive (retries ENOTCONN then succeeds) and negative (does not
retry PermissionDenied) unit tests against the inner read loop.

`POST /bootstrap/request` returned 403 Forbidden once the TEE first-boot
carve-out had already been claimed, but the documented API contract
requires 410 Gone. A 403 tells the caller "you specifically are not
authorized", which is the wrong signal for a single-use resource that no
caller, with any credentials, can ever claim again — 410 is what tells a
client the retry itself is pointless rather than "try different
credentials".

Adds `AppError::Gone` (renders as HTTP 410) to `vti-common`, alongside the
existing `Conflict`/`NotFound` variants, and switches both closed-carve-out
branches in `mint_mode_b` (the normal "sentinel already exists" check, and
the defensive concurrent-claim-loss path) onto a single
`carve_out_closed_error()` helper that returns it. This is a wire
compatibility fix, not a security fix — the carve-out was already correctly
refusing the second request; only the status code was wrong. The SDK's
`vta_sdk::error::VtaError::Gone` (mapped from HTTP 410 via `from_http`, with
an operator-facing "provision-integration a new operator instead" hint) was
already written expecting this status, so this closes the gap on the server
side.

Adds regression tests: `vti-common` pins the 410 status + body for the new
variant, and `vta-service` drives the real `mint_mode_b` end-to-end twice
against a simulated TEE provider (first call mints an admin and closes the
carve-out; second call, with a different client key and nonce, asserts
`AppError::Gone` / HTTP 410).

body:

* fix(tee): retry transient ENOTCONN on first vsock config-overlay read

tokio-vsock can report a stream connected just before Nitro finishes the

immediately, and the existing overall READ_TIMEOUT deadline still

Adds positive (retries ENOTCONN then succeeds) and negative (does not
retry PermissionDenied) unit tests against the inner read loop.

Signed-off-by: oleksii <oleksii.p@affinidi.com>

* fix(bootstrap): return 410 Gone for a consumed Mode B carve-out

`POST /bootstrap/request` returned 403 Forbidden once the TEE first-boot
carve-out had already been claimed, but the documented API contract
requires 410 Gone. A 403 tells the caller "you specifically are not
authorized", which is the wrong signal for a single-use resource that no
caller, with any credentials, can ever claim again — 410 is what tells a
client the retry itself is pointless rather than "try different
credentials".

Adds `AppError::Gone` (renders as HTTP 410) to `vti-common`, alongside the
existing `Conflict`/`NotFound` variants, and switches both closed-carve-out
branches in `mint_mode_b` (the normal "sentinel already exists" check, and
the defensive concurrent-claim-loss path) onto a single
`carve_out_closed_error()` helper that returns it. This is a wire
compatibility fix, not a security fix — the carve-out was already correctly
refusing the second request; only the status code was wrong. The SDK's
`vta_sdk::error::VtaError::Gone` (mapped from HTTP 410 via `from_http`, with
an operator-facing "provision-integration a new operator instead" hint) was
already written expecting this status, so this closes the gap on the server
side.

Adds regression tests: `vti-common` pins the 410 status + body for the new
variant, and `vta-service` drives the real `mint_mode_b` end-to-end twice
against a simulated TEE provider (first call mints an admin and closes the
carve-out; second call, with a different client key and nonce, asserts
`AppError::Gone` / HTTP 410).

Signed-off-by: oleksii <oleksii.p@affinidi.com>

* fix(bootstrap): finish the 410 contract, and scope the vsock retry to the handshake

Review follow-ups on #1003. No change to what the two original fixes do —
this closes the surfaces they left open.

410 / `AppError::Gone`

- `vta-backup`'s blob endpoints already declared `410` in both route
  annotations, and `ops::blob::gone()` carried a comment saying it had to
  approximate that with `Conflict` because no `Gone` variant existed. The
  variant exists now, so the helper returns it and the comment goes. This
  was the same defect the bootstrap half of this PR fixes: a documented
  410 that the code answered as something else. The
  ImportReceived/Previewed/Committed arm stays 409 — that bundle is
  progressing through the import flow, not consumed.
- Map `Gone` in the four error taxonomies that would otherwise have
  collapsed it into `internal-error` / `internalError` (`vta-service` and
  `vtc-service`, trust-task and DIDComm in each). It is reachable on
  neither transport today, but the fallback is the wrong default: a
  consumed single-use resource is a terminal caller-visible outcome, and
  reporting it as a server fault tells the client to retry something that
  can never succeed. No `e.p.msg.gone` wire code is invented for a variant
  no DIDComm surface produces; it rides with `conflict`.
- 410 now has more than one producer, so the CLI stops printing the
  bootstrap carve-out walkthrough for every one of them — an operator
  whose backup bundle expired was being sent to provision an admin. The
  hint is now selected on the refusal, and the 410 body goes through
  `extract_human_message` like the 409 body beside it.

vsock ENOTCONN

- Retry only while no byte has arrived. The constant and the commit
  message both say "the first read", but the arm sat inside the loop and
  applied to every one: a parent that dies mid-envelope would spin out the
  rest of READ_TIMEOUT and then report a timeout instead of the errno that
  explains it. Once a byte has arrived the connection demonstrably
  completed, so a later ENOTCONN is a real teardown.
- Log the retry once (latched, not once per 10ms tick). `connect_with_retry`
  warns per attempt; a boot that spent most of READ_TIMEOUT in the read
  must not look identical to one that read immediately.
- The mock becomes a scripted reader so the mid-stream case is testable,
  and pins that a hard error is not retried at all.

CI

- Run `routes::bootstrap` under `tee`. No job did: `tee` is not a default
  feature, so `cargo test --workspace` never built the module, and the
  `cargo check` step builds the lib only, so it never type-checked it
  either. Both properties in there are load-bearing — exactly one admin is
  ever minted, and a consumed carve-out refuses with a code that does not
  invite a retry — and neither was verifiable in CI.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.g@affinidi.com>

* fix(tee): accept ENOTCONN after complete overlay

Real Nitro can report ENOTCONN rather than EOF after the parent has delivered and closed a complete tenant-overlay envelope. Treat that close as transport completion only when the buffered bytes contain exactly one complete JSON value, then retain the existing strict version and allowlist parsing. Truncated payloads and unrelated I/O failures remain fail-closed.

Signed-off-by: oleksii <oleksii.p@affinidi.com>

title: test(vta): derive the unspecced fixture instead of naming one
body:
The salvage from #1018, which I closed as superseded by #1015. Two small things
that weren't in #1015; everything else there was a parallel rewrite not worth the
review time.

## The fixture that keeps rotting

`an_unspecced_task_proceeds_by_default_and_can_be_refused` needs a task with no
resolvable schema. It has been re-pinned **twice**: it named
`vta/webvh/dids/create/1.0` until trust-tasks #240 specified it, and #1015 moved
it to `vta/seeds/rotate/1.0` — which is itself on the keep-and-spec list, so the
next break is already scheduled.

Naming one is the problem. The fix each time is to name a different one, which
only sets up the next failure. #1015's own comment says exactly what to do:

> When `vta/seeds/*` is specified too, move this to whatever is still in
> `UNSPECCED_DISPATCHED_URIS` rather than weakening the assertion.

This does that mechanically. The fixture is now whatever is still unspecced at run
time, so the test follows the debt down instead of breaking each time a spec lands.

**The failure mode it replaces is the point.** A re-pinned test failing for a good
reason ("the thing you were testing got fixed") looks identical to a broken one,
and the tempting repair is to weaken the assertion — which would silently retire
the check that an operator can choose to fail closed. That warning is in #1015's
comment because the risk is real; this removes the occasion for it.

When the list finally empties, the test returns early with a note to delete it
along with the `require_payload_schema` escape hatch it exercises. That is the
honest end state — better than a fixture hunting for a task that no longer exists.

The payload also drops to `{}`. The task is unvalidatable by definition, so its
shape was never the property under test; a realistic-looking body implied it was.

## One annotation

The `api_integration` case that posts `"path_mode": { "mode": "auto_assign" }` with
snake_case member names. Since #1015 the SDK emits camelCase, which makes that case
**the only remaining test of the intake aliases** — and it now reads as staleness
someone would tidy away. Comment says so.

## Pre-merge

- [x] `cargo fmt --all`
- [x] `cargo clippy -p vta-service --all-targets` — clean
- [x] `cargo test -p vta-service --lib trust_tasks` — 139 passed
- [x] `cargo test -p vta-service --test api_integration` — 122 passed
- [x] No `version =` edits, no changelog file

title: feat(service): the vta/services task family, and the twenty routes it supersedes
body:
Completes the `/services/*` work: the eight handlers, then the twenty routes
they supersede. The operations are untouched — `operations::protocol::*`
already implements each transport — so this is the parameterised door onto
them, not new logic.

## One verb per task, not one per transport

`service` names the transport and `config` carries its settings, so the fan-out
happens in the handler rather than on the wire. Sixteen routes collapse onto
four tasks; a fifth transport needs a config variant, not four new specs.

## The drain guard is the part that matters

Tearing down a mediator discards whatever is in flight through it, so
`disable`/`update`/`rollback` on didcomm pass a `DisableTransport` deciding
whether the 1-hour floor applies. The REST route hardcodes `Rest` and the
DIDComm handler hardcodes `Didcomm` because each **is** that path. A trust task
is not, so it reads the arrival transport from the dispatch spine.

**The spine records confidentiality, not binding.** DIDComm and TSP are both
`EndToEnd` and it cannot tell them apart, so `EndToEnd` maps to `Didcomm` —
which *over-applies* the floor to a TSP-carried disable that doesn't strictly
need it.

That's deliberate, and the asymmetry decides it: under-applying tears down the
mediator a request arrived through and discards the reply to the very task
asking for it; over-applying only delays a teardown the operator can repeat.
The ambiguous case takes the cheaper mistake.

## Three shapes the generated types forced

- `ServiceMutationResult` and `RollbackKind` are **duplicated per family** —
  identical shapes, distinct types. Mutation results round-trip through the wire
  form rather than being hand-copied three times; rollback kinds go through a
  macro naming the variants, so divergence is a compile error.
- **Rollback may write nothing.** Its `noOp` arm has no `logEntryVersionId`,
  which is why it has its own result type — and the witness uses exactly that
  arm, so it's the case that breaks if the result ever starts requiring one.
- `handshake_timeout_secs` is `NonZeroU64` (the schema's `minimum: 1`), so the
  default is constructed, not unwrapped.

## Boxed futures, and why that's load-bearing

These handlers fan out to four sizeable operation futures, awaited inside a
dispatch match already carrying every other task's state machine. Inlining them
grew the frame past the default 8 MiB stack and **aborted an unrelated
`mock_vta` test with a stack overflow** — which reads as infinite recursion and
is not. `Box::pin` in the `op!` macro keeps the enclosing future flat.

I found this only because the abort didn't show up as a failed test: SIGABRT is
not a `test result: FAILED` line, so a naive grep reported zero failures on a
run that had stopped after 36 suites.

## Retry safety

Reads are `ReadOnly`; every mutation is `Keyed`, because each republishes an
append-only did:webvh log. `enable` refuses a transport already enabled, so a
repeat is a conflict rather than a duplicate — `Keyed` anyway, because a caller
who lost the reply **cannot tell that conflict from "it never landed"**, and the
cached response is what resolves it.

## The twenty routes (#1007's exclusion, lifted)

#1007 marked 56 routes and excluded `/services/*` for a stated reason: no twin
existed. It does now, so the metric covers the **whole** retirement-candidate
set rather than most of it. The mapping is derived from the route table, not
hand-written, and checked to leave nothing unmapped.

**The drain pair earns a test.** `/services/didcomm/drain` is one path serving
two operations — GET lists, POST cancels. They're the only pair sharing a path,
so they're the one entry a later edit could collapse by matching on path alone,
which would advertise a read as a destructive cancel or the reverse.

## Test

```
cargo test --workspace --features session,tsp   145 suites, 4525 passing
cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets -- -D warnings   clean
```

## Checklist (stack guide §9)

- [x] No new `reqwest::Client::new()` / bare `fetch()` (R1.2)
- [x] No lock held across a network await (R1.3)
- [x] No local state committed before its remote effect (R2.1)
- [x] **Every retry bounded + backed off; non-idempotent ops not blind-retried
      (R1.4)** — the retry-safety classifications above
- [x] Accept/poll/listen loops survive transient errors (R1.5)
- [x] Acks/deletes happen only after durable handoff (R1.6)
- [x] New/changed wire types: camelCase, schema registered (R3.*) — payloads and
      responses come from the generated types
- [x] Config absence = most restrictive (R5.*)
- [x] **Logs/status claim only what was verified (R6.\*)** — `drainUntil`
      reports what the agent actually did, never what the caller asked for
- [x] Deviations flagged with rule numbers

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.g@affinidi.com>

* feat(service): mark the twenty /services routes superseded

#1007 marked 56 routes and excluded `/services/*` for a stated reason: it had
no Trust-Task twin at all, so there was nothing to point the header at. The
family is specified now (trust-tasks #243) and the handlers land alongside
this, so the exclusion is over and the metric covers the whole retirement
candidate set rather than most of it.

Sixteen routes collapse onto four tasks, because the task is parameterised by
`service` — four verbs across four transports. The mapping is derived from the
route table rather than hand-written, and checked to leave nothing unmapped.

**The drain pair earns a test.** `/services/didcomm/drain` is one path serving
two operations: GET lists what is draining, POST cancels a drain. They are the
only pair in the table sharing a path, so they are the one entry a later edit
could collapse by matching on path alone — and collapsing them would advertise
a read as a destructive cancel, or the reverse. The test asserts both are
marked and that their successors differ.

Also corrects the table's own note, which said `/services/*` has no twin "and
needs specs first". True when #1007 wrote it; false now.

Workspace: 145 suites, 4525 passing. Clippy clean with --all-targets.
Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.g@affinidi.com>

* fix(service): gate the services family on webvh, as its operations already are

Feature combos caught what a workspace build cannot: `operations::protocol` —
every service operation these handlers call — is `#[cfg(feature = "webvh")]`,
because advertising a transport means editing the agent's did:webvh document.
Without webvh there is no document to edit, so the family goes with it. My
local builds always had webvh on, so the imports resolved and the gap stayed
invisible until CI ran `--no-default-features --features rest,didcomm`.

Three things needed the gate, and the third is the one worth explaining:

- the module,
- the eight dispatch entries, matching the webvh family already beside them,
- the eight conformance witnesses.

The witnesses matter because the sweep derives its census from what is actually
dispatched and requires the two to agree in BOTH directions. A witness for a
task that is configured out fails it exactly as a missing one does. They were
`vec!` elements, where `#[cfg]` does not apply, so the table now builds a Vec
and extends it conditionally — with the array typed explicitly, because
otherwise the element type comes from the first entry and each `parses::<T>` is
a distinct fn item rather than the `ParseFn` pointer the alias expects.

Verified against the exact combinations CI runs rather than the default
features: tee,rest,didcomm | rest,didcomm | aws-secrets,keyring,rest.

title: docs(pnm-cli): document the tsp and azure-secrets build features
body:
The README's Feature Flags table listed two of the crate's four features. Both omissions changed what an operator ends up with.

`tsp` is a default (`default = ["keyring", "tsp"]`) and gates the round-trip TSP probe in `pnm health`. The keyring-free build the README recommended, `--no-default-features --features config-session`, silently dropped it, after which `pnm health` reports an advertised `TSPTransport` service without ever exercising it. The build examples now re-add `tsp` and say why.

`azure-secrets` is off by default and inert unless `keyring` is also off — the backend's Azure arm is gated `not(feature = "keyring")` — so adding it to a default build selects nothing and reports no error.

The section also claimed "at least one of `keyring` or `config-session` must be enabled". Nothing enforces that. With neither, `default_backend` falls through to the plaintext file store and warns on every access, which is a materially different guarantee from the build-time gate the sentence implied. Replaced with the real selection order, `keyring` → `azure-secrets` → `config-session` → plaintext fallback, and the warning quoted verbatim.

Drive-by: the MSRV line said Rust 1.94.0+ where the workspace pins 1.95.0.

## Verification

- All three documented build combos compile: `cargo check -p pnm-cli`, `--no-default-features --features config-session,tsp`, `--no-default-features --features azure-secrets,tsp`.
- The fallback warning is real: `cargo run -p pnm-cli --no-default-features -- auth status` prints `WARNING: No secure session store — using plaintext file storage` verbatim (note the em dash — the README quotes it byte-for-byte).
- Not run: the `tsp`-off `pnm health` line, which needs a live TSP-advertising VTA. Verified by reading `pnm-cli/src/commands/health.rs:504`.

Docs-only; no `Cargo.toml`, no version, no changelog file. `cnm-cli/README.md` carries the same `azure-secrets` omission and the same false enforcement sentence — left for a follow-up.

title: chore(deps)!: move to trust-tasks-rs 0.11, and fix the wire drift it exposed
body:
Started as "did the sibling release fix the duplicate `trust-tasks-rs`?" — yes.
But the upgrade turns on schema validation for 22 tasks that previously had
none, and **three of them were sending non-conforming payloads**.

## The graph

`trust-tasks-https` / `-didcomm` / `-proof` / `-tsp` / `-capability-client` /
`-didcomm-v1` now all require `^0.11`, and `affinidi-messaging-sdk` 0.19.9 /
`-mediator` 0.18.20 followed. Until every one agreed, bumping the direct
dependency put **two** `trust-tasks-rs` nodes in the graph and the types crossed:

```
error[E0308]: expected `MediatorAcl`, found a different `MediatorAcl`
note: there are multiple different versions of crate `trust_tasks_rs`
```

Refreshing the lock to the versions that agree collapses it to one node.

## Three live defects, all the same class as #919

They were shipping before this PR. Nothing failed only because neither end had a
schema to check against.

1. **`CreateDidWebvhRequest` serialized snake_case.** Canonical wire is camelCase
   (R3.1) and the schema is `additionalProperties: false`. It worked solely
   through `CreateDidWebvhBody`'s back-compat aliases — which is exactly what made
   it invisible.
2. **`update_context` sent `null`** for unset members, where the schema types them
   as optional *strings*. Now built from `UpdateContextBody`, which skips `None`.
3. **`WebvhPathMode` emitted `auto_assign`** where the schema pins `autoAssign`
   with a `const` per `oneOf` branch.

**Number 3 is the one worth your attention.** The drift was in a *discriminant
value*, not a member name — so it slipped past every review and every convention
that watches member casing. And it was only reachable after fixing #1: the payload
had to get past the field-name check before the value check could fail. One drift
was hiding another.

Aliases keep the retired spellings accepted, so a peer built against the old shape
still parses; only what we **emit** moves. A round-trip test pins both directions,
and the REST test that posts the old spelling is annotated as the back-compat
coverage it now is — please don't let anyone "modernise" it.

## Four census guards, all shrinking

Every debt list in the workspace fired, each in the good direction:

| Guard | Change |
|---|---|
| manifest debt (`UNPUBLISHED_CANONICAL_OK`) | 36 → 14 |
| conformance witnesses | +22, each schema-validated with the mandatory non-vacuity check |
| `UNSPECCED_DISPATCHED_URIS` | −22 |
| producer-payload `UNPUBLISHED` | −2 |

I **de-rotted one test rather than re-pinning it**. `an_unspecced_task_proceeds_by_default`
hard-coded `webvh/dids/create` as its unspecced example — which this PR publishes,
so it failed for the best possible reason. It now derives one from the debt list at
runtime, so it follows the debt down instead of breaking every time a spec lands,
and returns early with a note to delete itself when the list empties.

## Follow-up I'd propose rather than bolt on

The 22 new witnesses use hand-written `json!`, which proves *the schema accepts a
shape*. Where a typed body exists (`CreateDidWebvhBody`, `UpdateContextBody`, …),
`to_v(typed)` is strictly stronger — it asserts **our types** conform, which is
what caught all three defects here. That's a second audit pass and will likely
surface more drift, so it deserves its own PR.

## BREAKING CHANGE

`WebvhPathMode` serializes as `wellKnown` / `autoAssign` instead of `well_known` /
`auto_assign`. Deserialization accepts both, so this breaks only a consumer that
string-matches on what we emit. Title carries `!`; expect the advisory semver job
to report it.

## Pre-merge

- [x] `cargo fmt --all --check` — clean
- [x] `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets` — clean
- [x] `cargo test --workspace --no-fail-fast` — **4514 passed, 0 failed** across 145 binaries
- [x] No `version =` edits, no changelog file

title: fix(sdk/service): take trust-tasks-rs 0.11, and fix the four defects it exposes
body:
## What this is

Moving to `trust-tasks-rs 0.11` brings the `vta/contexts/*` and `vta/webvh/*`
schemas into `schema_index`. **Everything else in this PR follows from that one
fact** — four separate guards refuse to let a task be dispatched against a
schema the registry now serves without being checked against it.

It also unblocks the `vta/services/*` handlers, which is what I set out to do;
those are a follow-up PR.

## Four real defects, none previously reachable by any test

Client-side `validate_payload` only runs for tasks whose schema resolves. Under
0.9 these four resolved to nothing, so the payloads went out unchecked. Each
would have been rejected by a conforming agent as `malformedRequest`:

| Defect | Why it matters |
|---|---|
| `create_did_webvh` sent `context_id`, `server_id`, `pre_rotation_count`, … | schema names `contextId` and forbids additional properties — **every** create over a task transport was malformed |
| `update_context` omitted `contextPolicy` entirely | a caller setting a policy had it silently accepted and never sent; **it failed by doing nothing** |
| `update_context` emitted `null` for unset members | bypassed `skip_serializing_if` via a hand-written `json!`; same shape as #919 |
| `WebvhPathMode` emitted `{"mode":"auto_assign"}` | schema's `oneOf` spells `autoAssign` |

The last one is worth separating from an ordinary casing slip: it's a
**discriminator value**. A `oneOf` keyed on `mode` matches *no branch*, so the
whole payload is malformed rather than oddly-spelled. It now emits camelCase
and accepts the old spelling via `alias`; its unit test was pinning the wrong
wire and now pins the right one plus the intake path.

Both `update_context` and `create_did_webvh` now build from their typed request
structs, so the wire comes from the same declaration the schema is generated
against and can't drift by hand again.

## 22 conformance witnesses

These families were dispatched against unpublished URIs, so the sweep skipped
them and they sat in `UNSPECCED_DISPATCHED_URIS`. They move out of that list and
into the witness table — which is what the list is *for*: it shrinks
monotonically as specs land.

**Written as raw JSON, not through the producer types, deliberately.** Two of
those producer types were wrong when the schemas arrived, so a witness built
from them would have encoded the defect and passed green. The schema is the
authority here, not the code that feeds it.

## The debt lists shrink

| | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| vtc-service unpublished bound URIs | 36 | **14** |
| `UNSPECCED_DISPATCHED_URIS` (contexts/webvh) | 22 | **0** |
| `producer_payload_conformance` UNPUBLISHED | 4 | **2** |

36 → 14 is the largest single fall that manifest count has taken. Its comment
already carried the history of the number moving, including a URI that went up
and back down in a day with the note *"That is the whole mechanism working, not
an exception to it."* I extended it rather than just editing the digit.

`an_unspecced_task_proceeds_by_default` needed a new fixture for the same
reason: it named `webvh/dids/create` as its example of an unspecced task, and
that task is now validatable, so its fail-closed half had stopped proving
anything.

## One witness I got wrong, caught by the round-trip check

I wrote `aclEntriesRemoved` / `aclEntriesUpdated` as counts. They're arrays of
ids. `every_witnessed_task_round_trips_through_its_generated_types` caught it —
exactly the hand-written-witness error class it exists for.

## Dependency chain behind this

This needed four upstream releases, each blocked on the last:
affinidi-tdk-rs#717 (`affinidi-messaging-sdk 0.19.9`, so `acl_setup`'s
`MediatorAcl` stops being a duplicated type) → trust-tasks #250 (the six
sibling crates, whose manifests required 0.11 while crates.io still served
tarballs built on 0.9).

## Test

```
cargo test --workspace --features session,tsp   4523 passing, 0 failures
cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets -- -D warnings   clean
```

## Checklist (stack guide §9)

- [x] No new `reqwest::Client::new()` / bare `fetch()` (R1.2)
- [x] No lock held across a network await (R1.3)
- [x] No local state committed before its remote effect (R2.1)
- [x] Every retry bounded + backed off (R1.4)
- [x] Accept/poll/listen loops survive transient errors (R1.5)
- [x] Acks/deletes happen only after durable handoff (R1.6)
- [x] **New/changed wire types: camelCase, schema registered, all consumers
      updated (R3.\*)** — the substance of this PR; four wire defects corrected
      against their published schemas, with `alias` on the discriminator so a
      producer mid-migration still parses
- [x] Config absence = most restrictive (R5.*)
- [x] Logs/status claim only what was verified (R6.*)
- [x] Deviations flagged with rule numbers

fix(sdk/service): take trust-tasks-rs 0.11, and fix the four defects it exposes (#1015)

* build(deps): move to trust-tasks-rs 0.11 and affinidi-messaging-sdk 0.19.9

trust-tasks-rs 0.11 carries the vta/services/* families this branch implements.
The move needed affinidi-messaging-sdk to go first — acl_setup hands a
MediatorAcl to TrustTasks::account_update, so two semver-incompatible copies of
trust-tasks-rs made that a type error rather than a link. That landed as
affinidi-tdk-rs#717 and published as 0.19.9.

vta-sdk builds clean on this. The workspace does NOT yet: vtc-service still
hits a duplicated TrustTask<Value> because the trust-tasks sibling crates
(trust-tasks-didcomm, -https, -proof, -tsp, -capability-client, -didcomm-v1)
changed their requirement to 0.11 without moving their own versions, so
crates.io still serves tarballs built against 0.9. dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf's
release/siblings-on-0.11 fixes that; this branch waits on it.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.g@affinidi.com>

* fix(sdk): two payload defects the 0.11 schema index made visible

Taking trust-tasks-rs 0.11 brings the vta/contexts and vta/webvh schemas into
`schema_index`, which turns on client-side validate_payload for tasks that had
no resolvable schema under 0.9. Two real defects surfaced immediately — both
would have been rejected by a conforming agent as malformedRequest, and neither
was reachable by any test before now.

**create_did_webvh sent snake_case.** `CreateDidWebvhRequest` predates the
schema published in trust-tasks #240 and carried `context_id`, `server_id`,
`pre_rotation_count`, `add_mediator_service`, `set_primary`. The schema names
`contextId` and friends and forbids additional properties, so every create over
a task transport was malformed:

    Additional properties are not allowed ('add_mediator_service', 'context_id',
    'pre_rotation_count', 'server_id', 'set_primary' were unexpected);
    "contextId" is a required property

**update_context dropped the policy and sent nulls.** Its payload was a
hand-written `json!` naming four members. It omitted `contextPolicy` entirely,
so a caller setting a policy had it silently accepted and never sent — the
worse of the two bugs, because it fails by doing nothing. And it read
`req.name`/`req.did`/`req.description` directly, bypassing their
`skip_serializing_if` and emitting `null` for each unset one, which the agent
refuses: an absent optional must be ABSENT, not null. That is the same shape as
#919.

Both now build from the typed request struct, so the wire comes from the same
declaration the schema is generated against and cannot drift from it by hand.

client_rest 86 passing.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.g@affinidi.com>

* fix(service): witness the 22 families 0.11 made checkable, and the defects they found

Taking trust-tasks-rs 0.11 brings the `vta/contexts/*` and `vta/webvh/*`
schemas into `schema_index`. Everything here follows from that one fact, and
none of it is optional: four separate guards refuse to let a task be dispatched
against a schema the registry now serves without being checked against it.

**22 conformance witnesses.** These families were dispatched against
unpublished URIs, so `schema_for` could not resolve them and the sweep skipped
them entirely — they sat in `UNSPECCED_DISPATCHED_URIS` instead. They now move
out of that debt list and into the witness table, which is what the list is
for: it shrinks monotonically as specs land.

The witnesses are written as raw JSON rather than through the producer types,
deliberately. Two of those producer types were WRONG when the schemas arrived,
so a witness built from them would have encoded the defect and passed green.
The schema is the authority here, not the code that feeds it.

**Two more producer defects, on top of the two already fixed.**

`WebvhPathMode` emitted `{"mode":"auto_assign"}` where the schema's `oneOf`
spells `autoAssign`. Worth separating from an ordinary casing slip: this is a
discriminator VALUE, and a `oneOf` keyed on `mode` matches no branch at all, so
the whole payload is malformed rather than oddly-spelled. It now emits
camelCase and accepts the old spelling on intake, and its unit test — which was
pinning the wrong wire — pins the new one and covers the alias.

The `preview-delete` witness first claimed `aclEntriesRemoved` and
`aclEntriesUpdated` were counts. They are arrays of ids. The round-trip check
caught it, which is exactly the class of hand-written-witness error it exists
for.

**The debt lists shrink.** 22 URIs off `UNSPECCED_DISPATCHED_URIS`, two off
`producer_payload_conformance`'s UNPUBLISHED census, and vtc-service's
unpublished-URI count falls 36 → 14 — the largest single fall that number has
taken. `an_unspecced_task_proceeds_by_default` needed a new fixture for the
same reason: it named `webvh/dids/create` as its example of an unspecced task,
and that task is now validatable, so the fail-closed half of it had stopped
proving anything.

Workspace: 4523 passing, clippy clean with --all-targets.
Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.g@affinidi.com>

* ci: retrigger the PR-title check after retitling

`commit lint` reads `github.event.pull_request.title`, but this workflow's
`on: pull_request` has no `types:`, so it defaults to opened/synchronize/
reopened — an edit does not retrigger it. Re-running the job does not help
either: a rerun replays the original event payload, so it would still read the
old title. Only a push produces a fresh payload.

The title was `fix(sdk,service): ...`; the scope charset is [a-z0-9._/-], so
the comma was rejected. It is now `fix(sdk/service): ...`.

Empty on purpose, and it disappears on squash-merge — which is the merge mode
this check exists to serve, since the PR title becomes the squash subject.

from vtc-service:

    error[E0308]: expected `TrustTask<Value>`, found a different `TrustTask<Value>`

a semver-incompatible move of that dependency is breaking for their consumers.

  trust-tasks-didcomm            0.9.0 -> 0.10.0
  trust-tasks-https              0.9.0 -> 0.10.0
  trust-tasks-proof              0.9.0 -> 0.10.0
  trust-tasks-tsp                0.9.0 -> 0.10.0
  trust-tasks-capability-client  0.8.0 -> 0.9.0
  trust-tasks-didcomm-v1         0.8.0 -> 0.9.0

The guard added in #245 should have caught this and did not. It watched
`trust-tasks-rs/src/specs` only, so a change that alters what a crate publishes
without touching its source — which is exactly what a dependency-requirement
bump is — was invisible to it. It now checks every publishable workspace member
